title: Man dies on Tasmania's west coast while waiting for ambulance
text:
A man on Tasmania's west coast has died while waiting for an ambulance which took nearly 80 minutes to arrive because of staffing issues, according to the state's health union.

The ABC understands the man, aged in his 60s, called Triple Zero (000) from the Zeehan area on Saturday, complaining of chest pains and issues breathing.

Health and Community Services Union state secretary Robbie Moore said this would be a "priority one" case, meaning an ambulance would try to get there "as soon as possible".

However, the ambulance in Zeehan was unstaffed on the day due to an unfilled gap in the roster, and the nearby crews in Strahan and Queenstown were responding to other calls, according to Mr Moore.

An ambulance in Burnie, about 140 kilometres north of Zeehan, was dispatched and arrived about 78 minutes after the Triple Zero call. However the man was dead when it arrived, the ABC understands.

Mr Moore said a crewed ambulance in Zeehan would have been able to arrive at the scene a "fair bit quicker than that".

"This is a very tragic situation that just highlights the need for the government to resource ambulance properly and to put on more permanent paramedics," Mr Moore said.

"Seventy-eight minutes is way too long to wait for somebody with chest pain — that's an emergency situation and it's likely to be a heart attack.

"You need an ambulance within 10 minutes to be able to give the best chance of survival and we weren't able to provide that due to a series of situations."

Mr Moore said he understood there had been a call out for volunteers to staff the Zeehan ambulance, but they "weren't able to get anyone".

Robbie Moore says more permanent paramedics are needed. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

The Department of Health has been contacted for comment.

Labor MP Ella Haddad said it was "absolutely unthinkable" that another person had died "because of cuts to the health budget".

"This really shines a light on the absolute dire need for investment in regional healthcare in Tasmania," Ms Haddad said.

The incident comes less than two weeks after an investigation was launched into the death of a man in Hobart, whose family had to transport him to hospital due to ambulance delays.

Tasmania's Health Minister, Bridget Archer, said this morning that she was not aware of any similar incidents involving ambulance delays.

"Any death that occurs is a tragedy and our hearts go out to any family and friends that are involved in that situation," Ms Archer said.

title: Car crushed by tree limb, lightning and 98 km winds in SA
text:
Wild weather has lashed South Australia over the weekend with almost 100 km per hour winds recorded in some areas like Port Augusta, while an Adelaide cafe saw a large tree branch smash the back of a parked car.

State Emergency Service (SES) state duty officer Ian Bonython said crews were called to 60 jobs from 7am Saturday over a 24-hour period.

"The majority of these tasking has been split between the northern Adelaide suburbs and the Port Augusta area," Mr Bonython said.

"With the taskings that came through for Port Augusta, around 20 were within half an hour."

Port Augusta received some wild weather over the weekend, with the SES being called to a lot of jobs involving wind damage and fallen trees. (Supplied: Leanne McGill)

He said the jobs were mainly wind-related, with crews dealing with fallen trees and structural damage to roofs and fences.

In Hyde Park in Adelaide's southern suburbs, restaurant owner Laura Edmunds said a large tree branch came down in their customer parking lot, completely crushing the back of a parked car.

"One of our chefs came running in and said, 'the tree's fallen again'," Ms Edmunds said.

Cafe owner Laura Edmunds said a tree limb crushed two cars parked in a Hyde Park car park. (ABC News)

"There was a little bit of a big crack and then just the noise of the car really... thank God no one was inside.

"[The] owner was pretty upset, she said it was a relatively new car but she was just very lucky, she's got a grandchild baby seat in the car, so she's very happy it didn't hit anyone."

A Hyde Park cafe owner said a fallen tree limb crushed two cars on Saturday. (ABC News)

The Hello Neighbour co-owner said the same tree had dropped limbs on a neighbouring business over six months ago.

The Bureau of Meteorology's David Crock said South Australia's weather had resulted from a tropical air mass over Queensland.

"[A] cold front off Southern Australia is picking up all that moisture and it's generated a rain band across South Australia, Victoria and Tasmania during early Sunday," Mr Crock said.

A storm rolls in at a station 40 kilometres west of Port Augusta. (Supplied: Scott Michael)

"We've seen rain and widespread storms across many parts of SA during Saturday and overnight into Sunday.

Mr Crock said wind gusts of 96-98 km per hour were recorded at various places late on Saturday, including Port Augusta where those wind gusts caused some damage.

"The rainfall for SA since 9am Saturday has reached 15-20mm through Adelaide and the hills, with some totals reaching 25 to 30mms around parts of eastern South Australia.

Scott Michael says hail, 21 millimetres of rain, and wind hit his station about 40 kilometres west of Port Augusta. (Supplied: Scott Michael)

"There's plenty more rain on the way to Adelaide today, clearing out later as the system moves towards the eastern states."

SA Power Networks spokesperson Celia Schutz confirmed about 12,000 customers lost power from midday Saturday to 10 am this morning.

"Approximately 500 customers are currently without power," Ms Schutz said.



"SA Power Networks crews continue work to restore customers impacted overnight across the Eyre Peninsula, mid north, south east and metropolitan area."

title: Midwest muso Kevin Morby is no longer America's best kept secret
text:
During the 2020 pandemic, US singer-songwriter Kevin Morby almost got stuck in Australia.

As quarantines tightened, he found himself in Melbourne before it had some of the world's toughest lockdowns.

He didn't panic. Instead, he remembers thinking:

" If I have to start a new life, this is a pretty good place to do so. "

He has become acquainted with Australia's bigger cities over multiple visits.

"Feel[ing] like, 'Oh, I know where I'm at. I know this neighbourhood — I love that one restaurant! It's nice," he tells Double J's Henry Wagons.

Double J — a place for music lovers Double J gives you the new music you'll actually love, alongside the classic tracks you keep coming back to. Give your playlist a rest and join us here.

That moment of acceptance speaks to something essential about Morby, a folk-rock journeyman who finds belonging and meaning in transit.

That philosophy feels more relevant than ever as Morby returns to tour Australia next month, supporting his latest album Little Wide Open.

Following a discography inspired by adopted homes — Laurel Canyon (2016's Singing Saw), New York (2017's City Music), Memphis (2022's This Is A Photograph) — Morby's eighth solo album heads back to the Missouri farmlands and Kansas City suburbs where he grew up.

"I have a complicated relationship to it, just as most people do with their home towns. There's a lot of love and a lot of resentment. It's all these emotions and a lot of them come out on this record."

Kevin Morby plays shows around Australia in November. (Supplied: Chantal Anderson)

The Midwest and musical influences

A collection of sentimental alt-country, dusky folk and lush Americana, Little Wide Open conjures rich imagery: fields of sunflowers and June bugs, late-night bars and long highways stretching into flat horizons dominated by wide open skies.

Porchside strumming and finger-picking score vivid portraits of "anywhere America" on songs with names like Cowtown and Bible Belt.

Small-town iconography and spangling riffs power 100,000, before a guitar explodes like a Fourth of July firecracker over the song's climax.

These tunes, built from tried-and-true chords and Morby's humble Dylanesque voice, romanticise the comforts of small towns but equally yearn to escape them for something larger.

Loading Instagram content

For Morby, the Midwest is simple.

"I don't mean that in a derogatory sense. The lifestyles are simpler. There's a quality of life, your money goes further, things like that. But with that, there's less opportunity and less culture.

"There can be great things about the Midwest.

" I feel if you use the time and space and the boredom to your advantage, those don't have to necessarily be bad things. "

You can hear the influence of Morby's "big five": Bob Dylan, Leonard Cohen, Lou Reed, Nina Simone, and Townes Van Zandt.

But also, more pluck and twang ("Country music's great. One of [music's] backbones over the past two centuries") as well as the "rootsy, heartland rock and roll" Morby was immersed in making the record.

"I bought this pick-up truck with a free subscription to satellite radio. Part of that was the Tom Petty radio station and I just got super into him. He was a big influence."

Loading SoundCloud content

He also cites the album World Without Tears by legendary artist Lucinda Williams, who provides a drawling, cautionary spoken word on stand-out track Natural Disaster.

"I wanted this voice-of-God thing to come in. I was so thrilled when she said she'd do it."

Williams isn't Little Wide Open's only notable guest.

Famous friends

In a sign of how esteemed Morby is among his peers, the album also features Bon Iver's Justin Vernon (emulating a tornado siren on rustic opener Badlands), backing vocals from MUNA's Katie Gavin, and players from Florence + The Machine, Perfume Genius, Sylvan Esso and Hand Habits.

Then there's The National's Aaron Dessner. Fresh from producing blockbuster records for Taylor Swift and Ed Sheeran, Dessner recorded Little Wide Open at his studio in upstate New York.

"He made the songs feel big and dense in their ways without distracting the story or the vocal," Morby explains.

"He really kept my vocal front and centre. It felt like I was standing a little bit naked on these recordings, but I think it benefited the album in the end.

"Besides that, he's just an unbelievable musician. And really believed in these songs through moments where maybe I wasn't believing in them … 'Kevin, you gotta let these songs breathe.'"

Dessner's fingerprints are all over Junebug, with its gossamer guitars and piano decorated by oboe and harp. But those flourishes never overshadow Morby.

"Sometimes the myth grows bigger than the dream" he sings on the swooning title track, where banjo, slide guitar and fiddle comfortably sprawl past the eight-minute mark.

Getting older (and better)

Little Wide Open is also charged by Morby "looking down the barrel of 40," and the sense of life moving too fast.

"Am I a has-been? Am I a husband?" he sings ruefully amid the otherwise upbeat Javelin. Nearly cut for being too vulnerable, the lyric was prompted by impending parenthood.

Morby recently welcomed his first child alongside his musician-partner Katie Crutchfield, better known as alt-country favourite Waxahatchee.

"We fell in love on tour. We're these creative sounding boards for one other. I really trust Katie's ear and her thoughts. It's real easy to walk in the other room and say, 'Hey, is this lyric good?'"

Loading Instagram content

While she doesn't feature on Little Wide Open, "Katie is very much in the DNA. It's a lot of love songs," Morby says.

"It's a funny thing being in a public relationship because people are going to know who you're singing about."

Because Morby's music is presented with such easy-going charm, you can easily miss the serious subject matter of his lyrics, which contemplate existential questions about life, time and mortality.

"It's a darker song [but] for the longest time, I wanted to call the record I Ride Passenger," Morby says of a tune loosely inspired by a fan who died in a car crash on his way to see him perform.

The central lyric? "If time is a violent driver, then we ride passenger."

Loading Instagram content

Die Young is a warm, mid-tempo reflection on aging, and surviving the fragile existence of a touring musician.

That idea is revisited on the plaintive closer, Field Guide for The Butterflies, which uses insects splattered on windshields as a metaphor for troubadours compelled to reach and share deeper truths despite the risks of lonely lives spent on the road.

But "it's not suicide if I die out chasing thrills" Morby confides in the album's closing moments. "Just me trying to grow wings."

It's a moving finish to a record where Morby ponders where he's been, what happens next and what it all means.

Kevin Morby's tour begins in Eltham on Thursday, November 12, before shows in Bellingen, Brisbane, Mt Glorious, Sydney, Brunswick Heads, Castlemaine and Melbourne.

title: Antonelli on pole as he eyes record-setting world F1 title
text:
Kimi Antonelli has blasted to pole position for the United States Grand Prix on a weekend when he could claim his place as Formula One's youngest world champion.

The 20-year-old Italian turned the tables on Ferrari as the Scuderia, who had led the way for all three practice sessions, again fell flat when it came to the crunch on Sunday AEST.

Antonelli pipped Max Verstappen, winner of the past two races, to first spot on the grid by 0.179 seconds, with Isack Hadjar third in the second Red Bull.

Australia's Oscar Piastri and his McLaren teammate Lando Norris managed seventh and eighth respectively.

How Kimi Antonelli can win the F1 title Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli can secure his maiden Formula 1 drivers' championship with victory at the United States Grand Prix.

For Antonelli to claim the crown in the Lone Star State is a tall order; he would need to win Monday's race (AEST) and hope that George Russell finishes lower than ninth and Lewis Hamilton lower than fifth.

But he did the first part of his job in supreme fashion, delivering a stellar lap to blow away his rivals and underline why he is the champion-in-waiting.

Russell struggled and will line up sixth, while Charles Leclerc and Hamilton managed only fourth and fifth as Ferrari's pace disappeared when it mattered.

The race represents 20-year-old Antonelli's first shot at clinching the crown, but with a 102-point lead and only a maximum 150 left up for grabs, it appears merely a matter of when the Italian becomes champion.

Ferrari have not been on pole since Leclerc in Hungary in 2025, while Hamilton's wait for top spot in qualifying extends to that same race two years earlier, 1,190 days ago.

Hamilton is a five-time winner around the Circuit of the Americas and an upgraded Ferrari appeared to have put him in the mix to end his long wait for a pole position.

Ferrari president John Elkann was watching on from the garage, with pressure on the team to finally deliver in qualifying after a difficult run of races and increased speculation over the future of team principal Fred Vasseur.

This weekend could be bigger than Texas for Kimi Antonelli if he can clinch the world title. (Getty Images: Clive Mason)

But Hamilton, 41, whose sole Ferrari win came in Barcelona in June, and Leclerc were again unable to pull it out of the bag.

Meanwhile, both Williams were among the stragglers knocked out in Q1 as their miserable season continued, with Alex Albon fuming "what a s***show".

Norris topped Q1 but McLaren chief executive Zak Brown told Sky Sports that Ferrari were "in a league of their own".

Leclerc hit back to lead Q2 but Antonelli and Russell had also come to the fore to suggest the battle for pole would be a tight one.

Antonelli soared to the top of the charts after the first run in Q3 and the Italian's challengers fell by the wayside.

AAP/PA

title: WA government to consider return of Perth to Albany passenger rail service
text:
The WA government's plan to buy back the state's freight rail network has opened the door for a passenger train from Perth to Albany to also be introduced.

Communities in the Great Southern region say a passenger train would help connect towns to vital services as well as boost tourism.

The Great Southern Railway, built in the 1900s, stretches 450 kilometres from Perth to the city of Albany, and passes through half a dozen towns including Narrogin, Wagin, Katanning, Tambellup and Mount Barker.

There have been several attempts to bring back the passenger line since it was scrapped in 1978, but none has been successful.

Passengers boarding a train at the Mount Barker train station in 1910. (Supplied: State Library of Western Australia)

Push for passenger rail

Rail advocacy group Countrynet Rail Alliance says the state buyback of the freight network presents an opportunity to revive both agricultural and passenger services.

"As part of the buyback, I think it is time to actually take a really good look at this from an economic perspective and to look at all of the potential gains and benefits that could come from it," spokesperson Simon Lyas said.

"It's cheaper to do it now than it will be in 10 or 20 years, and I think that's why it warrants a particularly special investigation and feasibility study to find out what the costs would be and what the benefits would be."

The state government said bringing the regional rail network back under public control was its top priority. It has shown in-principle support for the return of a Great Southern passenger rail.

"Public control of the network will allow for the consideration of new passenger rail opportunities," a spokesperson for Transport Minister Rita Saffioti said.

"However, passenger rail requires significant investment, both in terms of capital expenditure and ongoing operational costs, to make it a viable alternative to road transport."

The proposal has received support from the City of Albany and other major regional towns along the route.

Tourism offering

Albany Mayor Greg Stocks, who recalls travelling on the original passenger train line as a 16-year-old, said the community had long hoped for the return of the service.

Greg Stocks says there is support for a passenger service to return to Albany. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

"We certainly support it … there are a lot of people in Albany who would like to see the return of that service," he said.

Mr Stock said the line would benefit businesses in the city that catered to tourists but also support the wider economy of the Great Southern region.

"I think there might be a unique tourism offer on that and the experience of actually going through the hinterland as well," he said.

"There are a lot of shires along that railway line that are very keen to see it happen, so there'll certainly be benefit for them as well."

Mr Stocks said the city supported a feasibility study, but it was already seeking funding from the state on other priorities such as housing, health, roads and education.

Vital lifeline

Katanning Shire President Kristy D'Aprile said a passenger train line would help those residents between Perth and Albany who struggled to access social services in the country.

Kristy D'Aprile says a passenger line would connect Katanning residents to vital services. (Landline: Anthony Pancia)

"Katanning struggles with health care and education and those things that are very typical of a smaller regional community," she said.

" Having a passenger rail service will allow our community access to those services that are likely going to be based in either Albany or in Perth. "

Ms D'Aprile said the line would also support industry and agricultural businesses in Katanning, one of the Great Southern economic and industrial hubs, to attract and retain workers.

"Often, they are coming down to work in either our abattoir or on our farms. So having a reliable, regular passenger rail network will enhance accessibility for our employees and our workforce," she said.

Curtin University professor of sustainability Peter Newman said there was a strong case for bringing back the passenger rail by looking to other jurisdictions across the country.

Peter Newman says regional rail has worked well in other states. (ABC News: Briana Shepherd)

"Trains are very popular … they work, and that's now on the agenda in country towns," he said.

"Other states in Australia like New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, they've got far more of that country service running, and it's really helping those country towns."

title: Have your cake and eat Freo too at this sweet design event
text:
An event looking at Fremantle through the lens of sponge cake, jelly, and plenty of icing has encouraged people to see, and taste, the city differently.

Cakemantle, an event held as part of Fremantle Design Week, was the brainchild of designers Loren Holmes and Rosie Halsmith, who invited the public to both make and come and taste dessert creations inspired by the port city.

The organisers didn't give any guidance to the bakers other than that the cakes "had to be edible and they had to be able to talk about why they chose that place", Ms Holmes said.

Cakemantle organisers Loren Holmes and Rosie Halsmith. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

Sixteen entrants rose to the challenge, some professional designers, others locals who were inspired to say something about Freo.

The result was a rich tapestry of the city. Some entrants made recognisable interpretations of well-known landmarks like Monument Hill, the (car carrier ship) Wallenius Wilhelmsen and the old Roundhouse prison.

Others explored the city in time, one re-imagining the rocky bar at the river mouth that was removed to create Fremantle Harbour as a shipping port, another imagined the city several hundred years in the future, after the seas have risen and fallen.

The slab tells the little-known history of the morgue at Bathers Beach, the pavilion now attached to an arts centre. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

One family effort, featuring two small white figures lying on a slab under a pitched canopy, shared a little-known slice of history.

"It's a reference to the morgue that used to be at Bathers Beach," maker Vanessa said.

"It's a bit of a play on words with the slab, like a slab of cake and also the slab where the bodies used to be.

"That was where we got our inspiration from, and we kind of liked the idea because it's a place we all go to often, but a lot of people don't know all the history and stories."

The Scolaro Terrazzo cake came second in the competition. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

Another entrant, produced by members of a Perth landscape design studio, painstakingly used cheesecake, jelly, cake and local bush ingredients to recreate pieces of terrazzo tile, produced by Italian immigrants Giuseppe and Anna Scolaro at their Fremantle factory.

The cake was instantly recognisable as terrazzo tile that was a popular feature of many buildings from the 1950s until the 70s, and which is now experiencing a resurgence in popularity.

But before the crowd, who had reserved eating tickets to the event, could conduct a taste test, there was a competition to run.

Three judges, executive chef Blaze Young, landscape architect Scott Lang and UWA dean of design Sarah McGann, were asked to judge the entries on three criteria — taste, idea and execution.

The judges taste all 16 cakes entered in Cakemantle. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

It proved a tough task, Scott Lang said, not just because it involved sampling 16 pieces of cake but because the concepts were highly original.

"It was actually super tough," he said.

"The ideas that people have come up with and the way they were thinking about Fremantle was pretty amazing and the execution of how they were representing those ideas.

"For me it was the ones that could really come up with a very clear and simple, strong idea about what is special about Fremantle, that's what I was most impressed by."

When the votes were tallied, third place went to a cake called the Fremantle Doctor, a rendering of the afternoon sea breeze in human form, with a flowing blue beard, which judge Blaze Young praised as having a "beautiful balance of flavours".

16 people entered Cakemantle, and many more got tickets to taste. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

In second place was the Scolaro Terrazzo tiles creation, which was singled out for its design and execution.

In first place was Erin Coates, who reimagined the former limestone rock bar at the mouth of the Derbarl Yerrigan/Swan River, which the judges praised for its exceptional taste.

"As soon as we tasted it, it was really the flavour that pushed it over the edge," Mr Young said.

"I think I would be quite proud to put something like this on the menu at my restaurant."

Loren Holmes with the winning entry, Erin Coates' rocky limestone bar that was removed from the river mouth. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

Ms Coates was delighted.

"I'm so thrilled because I'm not really much of a baker," Ms Coates said after the announcement.

"The cake is based on my interest in the geology and the habitats underneath the surface of the river.

"I dive quite a lot and I free-dive a lot in the river and looked at the changing ecology there and this cake is a re-imagining of that space if C.Y. O'Connor hadn't removed the rock bar at the mouth of the river."

This family entry re-imagined Walyalup Koort (Kings Square) in Fremantle reclaimed by nature. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

After the awards were given out, it was time for eating.

Ms Holmes said given how quickly tickets sold out, both to people wanting to bake and those wanting to eat, the organisers were hoping to bring the event back next year.

"We think that there might be more. I think given the popularity of this one, we reckon it might be a recurring event in the Fremantle Design Week calendar."

title: Volkanovski underscores UFC greatness with record ninth title win
text:
Australian Alexander Volkanovski has underlined his greatness with a stunning second-round TKO of previously unbeaten Russian Movsar Evloev in a record-extending ninth UFC featherweight title fight win.

Headlining the UFC 333 card in Abu Dhabi, Volkanovski was considered the underdog in some quarters, but the 38-year-old proved too good for his younger opponent, the number one contender.

He got Evloev down to the ground with some precise, hurtful punching and landed some brutal ground and pound to force referee Marc Goddard to stop the fight with six seconds of the second round remaining.

Volkanovski, from Windang on the NSW South Coast, landed with some good kicks and punches in the first couple of minutes.

Elite wrestler Evloev (20-1) took Volkanovski down three times in the last couple of minutes of the first round, but the Australian quickly bounced back to his feet each time.

The champion had a cut on his face in the second round, but in the last few seconds he bloodied Evloev's face, as his crisp, accurate punches found their mark.

It was his first stoppage win in six fights stretching back to 2023.

"It feels good to get a finish," said Volkanovski, who improved his MMA record to 29-4.

"I actually promised the missus, it was our wedding anniversary on Wednesday, I promised her a quick one (win) so she wasn't stressing on the sidelines."

It was a second successful defence of his second reign and Volkanovski indicated he wasn't ready to retire yet.

"I said if I didn't take too much damage, we'll probably keep going, so maybe we keep going," Volkanovski said.

Movsar Evloev had no answer to Volkanovski's attacks. (Getty Images: Zuffa LLC/Jeff Bottari)

Evloev landed some good strikes but couldn't maintain the pressure on the wily champion.

"He's like good wine; older, stronger, better, he's truly a legend," Evloev said.

In a thrilling co-main event, Russia's Petr Yan retained the bantamweight world title with a unanimous points decision over Georgia's Merab Dvalishvili, beating him for the second time in three fights.

In the prelims, Australians recorded a win and two losses against Russian opponents.

Volkanovski's stablemate, bantamweight Colby Thicknesse, scored a third straight win and a big upset with a split-decision victory over previously unbeaten Asaf Chopurov.

Middleweight Cam Rowston's run of seven straight wins ended with a first-round guillotine-choke-submission loss to 12th-ranked Abus Magomedov of Russia, and middleweight Jacob Malkoun's three-fight win streak was snapped by a unanimous-points loss to Abubakar Vagaev.

AAP

title: Australian 11yo brings home gold from snooker and eight ball championships
text:
At just 11 years old, Angelo Tsikouris is a champion with six national titles under his belt.

But his choice of sport is not necessarily a popular one with his age group — Angelo plays a gentleman's sport: snooker.

He says he developed a love of the game by watching his grandfather play.

"When I was about five, he used to put me on the ground and I'd shoot a ball through a toilet roll," Angelo says.

Angelo Tsikouris already has six national titles under his belt. (ABC News: Tilda Colling)

He snuck his first game on a table at home when his dad was out grocery shopping and has been inseparable from the cue sport since.

His mother Natalie Tsikouris says initially they didn't realise how talented Angelo was, but at nine years old he won the national under-12s competition.

At first, Angelo Tsikouris's family didn't realise just how talented he was at snooker. (ABC News: Tilda Colling)

"When he won, we were like: Did he, did he just win?" Ms Tsikouris says.

" It's a huge achievement but it's more that he kept doing it, kept winning again. "

Angelo went on to win three national junior titles in snooker and another three in eight ball last week while on a trip to the UK to represent Australia in the international blackball championships.

He wants more kids to take up table sports — specifically snooker.

"I'm the only one in Darwin that's playing snooker, or the NT," he says.

Angelo Tsikouris wants more NT kids to take up snooker. (ABC News: Tilda Colling)

Another young champ

Angelo may be the Territory's sole young snooker champ, but he's not the only local kid with a gift for playing table sports.

Fifteen-year-old Adam Grace is the best eight ball player in the Northern Territory — and that includes adult players.

At just 15, Adam Grace is the best eight ball player in the NT. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"I practise two or three hours after school, and that's every day," he says.

"I don't really do that much homework, mainly pool."

Adam travelled to Norway earlier this year to represent Australia in the under-19s category.

"It gives me really good confidence when I shoot a ball, I just like the sound of it going into the pocket," he says.

Given how many hours he practises each day, Adam says there's not much time for homework. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

He will represent the NT at the national eight ball championships later this year, as its youngest-ever champion.

Ken Kernich, president of the Northern Territory Eight Ball Association, says there are a handful of other young Territorians who also compete in cue sports at an international level.

As for why the Territory is home to so many child champions, he has one theory.

Ken Kernich says the local young guns undergo plenty of practise to hone their skills. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"Maybe an air-conditioned room where you can play pool is a lot better than working out in the sunshine," he says.

"But they commit themselves to being good players, they practise, practise, practise.

"A lot of people struggle to get one ball into a pocket, [but] when you practise that much it's almost like putting marbles into buckets."

title: Qualified migrant women forced into 'survival jobs' are paying price
text:
Despite four years of experience in accounting when she lived in Afghanistan, Farukh Tahery had to start from scratch when the Taliban took over in 2021 and she moved to Australia.

"When I came to Australia, I found out, yes, finding a job is hard," she said.

"Every time I received feedback from employers, they told me that 'You're not qualified'… I was feeling [like] I'm not enough."

Ms Tahery had experience in accounting before migrating to Australia. (ABC News)

Recent research from not-for-profit Settlement Services International (SSI) found migrant women in Australia were 20 per cent more likely than migrant men to be over-qualified in a job.

It took about a year living in Australia before Ms Tahery found work, with support from SSI.

She worked at The Social Outfit, a fashion brand based in Newtown, which hires refugee and migrant women, training them in retail and the industry.

Ms Tahery found work at The Social Outfit with help from Settlement Services International. (ABC News)

Ms Tahery learnt how to make sales, mail orders, and recently, helped design a new line of clothes, which included a skirt worn by Governor-General Sam Mostyn.

However, Ms Tahery said fashion was not a "long-term career" for her.

"I finished a Certificate IV of Accounting and Bookkeeping at TAFE, and I tried to find a job [but] I couldn't, and then I started a Diploma of Accounting. I'm trying to get that qualification to find a job as an accountant," she said.

Ms Tahery helped design clothes, including a skirt worn by the Governor-General Sam Mostyn (right). (ABC News: Isla Evans, Supplied: Koshka Media)

Forced to navigate 'fragmented system'

About 340,000 migrant women working in Australia were employed below their skill level, SSI research showed.

Malini Raj, Executive Director of the Australian Multicultural Women's Alliance (AMWA), said migrant women unable to get their overseas qualifications recognised in Australia were forced into "survival jobs".

"And therefore they're in a cycle of lower income, lower superannuation, and lower long-term prospects," she said.

"There's psychologists, engineers, teachers, nurses, all unable to get their qualifications recognised because of a costly, time consuming and complicated process."

Malini Raj says the process to get skills recognised in Australia is fragmented. (ABC News: Isla Evans)

Ms Raj said it takes a woman with overseas GP qualifications an average of $50,000 and two years to get recognition and work in Australia.

"They're forced to navigate a fragmented system on their own, and therefore, they don't have a clear pathway to get their skills recognised.

" And the longer they are away from their jobs, the harder it is to get back into their profession. "

Eager to work

Consuelo Castillo migrated to Australia from Chile with seven years of teaching experience, a bachelor's degree in secondary education, and a master's degree in early childhood and primary education.

"When I first started to look for jobs here … my only option was working as an assistant in after-school care," she said.

Consuelo Castillo migrated to Australia with qualifications and experience in teaching. (ABC News: Isla Evans)

Finding work, she added, was like trying to get "behind closed doors".

"The most common answer was, 'You have to restart what you already know'."

While Ms Castillo enjoys her current role as an early childhood teacher, she hoped for a more linear pathway, and said the current system was "creating problems within itself".

"Classrooms have more students and less teachers, and [there are] teachers with more workloads, when we could be there helping them," she said.

Waiting for a chance

SSI and AMWA have called for a national commissioner to be appointed to oversee the skills recognition process for new migrants and refugees.

Ms Raj said it takes years for most migrant women in Australia to get their qualifications recognised.

"We also have skills shortage in those professions which they are qualified for," she said.

"We've invited them into the country for those skills, so it's time that we recognise them."

Ms Tahery is studying at TAFE with the aim of getting a job in accounting. (ABC News: Isla Evans)

Ms Tahery hopes to find her way back to accounting once she has completed her TAFE qualifications.

"If [employers] accept the qualifications that we bring with us, if they gave us a chance to show that, 'Yes, we can do it', that would make everything easier," she said.

title: We both overpromised our physical attributes in an email. It led to love
text:
When Vyshnavee met Thiru on email he promised her movie star looks and she promised him a body-building physique. Vyshnavee writes that both underdelivered, but the email did lead to love.

Whether it's romantic, platonic, heartbreaking or surprising, our Love Story series is about love in all its forms. Share yours with us.

I've known my husband Thiru for almost a third of my life.

We met on a blind date in 2011; set up by a mutual friend via email e-intro (a forgotten era before dating apps).

The first sign of genuine chemistry was the ease of banter.

In an attempt to provide physical descriptors, he referred to himself as a dark-skinned Brad Pitt. In return, I told him I possessed the musculature of a female bodybuilder.

Both of these were gross embellishments of course, and I couldn't resist looking him up on Facebook before we met.

A Sri Lankan Adam Brody may have been a more accurate depiction (everybody wants this).

Our first date was at Grasshopper Bar — a pioneer of the small bar scene in Sydney — located just off George St in the CBD. Caught up in our conversation, we hung out until the early hours, right until the bar closed.

Vyshnavee says her relationship with Thiru is grounded in friendship and emotional security. (Supplied: Vyshnavee Wijekumar)

A differing worldview, despite shared heritage

Despite having shared Sri Lankan Tamil heritage, Thiru and I grew up very differently, which shaped our perspective on the Australian identity and our place within it.

He grew up in Sydney's Northern Beaches, at a time when cultural diversity was virtually non-existent. I grew up in Western Sydney, surrounded by the continual waves of newly arrived migrant and refugee communities.

As our worlds merged, this friction felt pronounced.

When Thiru would often venture across the Harbour Bridge to see me, he was treated to authentic and affordable dine-out options from a broad array of cultures.

When I hung out with him in Narrabeen and Manly, I could feel the enquiring eyes of locals staring at me.

The ease of banter was one of the first signs of the chemistry between Vyshnavee and Thiru. (Supplied: Vyshnavee Wijekumar)

His way of countering racism was to educate: explaining why Hindus were vegetarian on a Friday or correcting his rugby team that he was in fact Sri Lankan, not Aboriginal. He even had a teacher call him Wendell after South Sea Islander / West Indian rugby player, Wendell Sailor.

We'd often have heated debates about the discrimination experienced in our daily lives.

He'd chalk it up to ignorance. I, on the other hand, would be less forgiving, asserting those that didn't possess racial literacy should use Google.

I was raised with a strong connection to my Sri Lankan Tamil identity, while still appreciating Australian culture (Kylie Minogue was the highlight of the AFL grand final). My family was active in the Sri Lankan community, and I spoke my mother tongue at home.

Thiru was brought up being immersed in Australian culture, and whenever he would attempt to speak Tamil, his mum would tell him to stop butchering her language.

In a way, he grew up feeling like he wasn't quite Australian or Sri Lankan enough.

There was also the chasm of class.

I came from a working-class suburb with a high crime rate, which instilled a strong sense of social justice in me. Coming from an affluent area, Thiru was surprised I wasn't constantly seized by abject fear.

The differences in our upbringings created conflict and understanding in equal measure.

He would pull me out of my bubble, pushing me to justify my views; and I made him feel at one with his Tamil identity.

Vyshnavee and Thiru have been through their share of challenges and milestones together including fertility struggles. (Supplied: Vyshnavee Wijekumar)

We've come a long, long way together

A 15-year relationship has led to a lot of shared milestones and challenges: moving interstate, marriage, therapy, home ownership, fertility struggles (mine) and an ADHD diagnosis (his).

His once-luscious curls have retreated into a receding hairline, and the toned physique I once boasted has descended into postpartum softness.

There are still major differences: he has a deep love of sports, while I'm passionate about the arts. Though, in truth, he's accompanied me to more theatre shows than I've attended cricket games.

As I've watched many friends end long-term relationships, I've queried what keeps us together — and not in a smug way. Our relationship is by no means perfect, but somehow, amongst life's logistical tango, there's an underlying friendship and emotional security that's helped us persevere through it all.

And in the modern age of ghosting and love bombing, that kind of love is ageless.

title: Sam Konstas cracks yet another century
text:
Sam Konstas has struck his second century in the space of a week to send national selectors yet another reminder he is ready for a Test recall.

Just days after posting scores of 71 and 151 not out in New South Wales' Sheffield Shield draw with Western Australia, Konstas cracked 149 off 131 balls on Saturday to lead his side to a 78-run victory over the Warriors in the One-Day Cup at the WACA Ground.

NSW posted 8-371 on the back of the monster knock from Konstas combined with handy contributions from Josh Philippe (51), Jack Edwards (45) and Lachlan Shaw (44).

In reply, Sam Whiteman plundered 116 from 113 balls to give WA a faint hope of chasing down the mammoth victory target.

But with spinner Ashton Agar (43) and Ashton Turner (41) the only other WA batters to pass 40, the home side fell well short of what was required, bowled out for 293 in 46.3 overs.

The result left WA with a 0-3 record, all but ending its title hopes just three games into the season.

NSW moved into second spot with a 3-1 record.

But it remains to be seen how much longer its will have Konstas in its Shield and one-day ranks given his rich vein of form.

The 21-year-old burst onto the international scene in December 2024 when he made a memorable Boxing Day Test debut against India, scoring 60 in his maiden knock.

Konstas failed to pass 25 in his next nine Test innings, with his most recent appearance in the baggy green coming in July last year against the West Indies.

Awkward questions linger after Australian loss It is a case of the same old problems leading to the same old questions as Australia squanders a series lead, setting up a grandstand finale in South Africa next week.

The talented opener has worked hard on his game over the past 15 months, and it was on full display on Saturday as he cracked 15 fours and four sixes in a masterful display.

And with Australia still crying out for an opener to make his mark ahead of a busy Test schedule, it seems just a matter of time before Konstas is donning the baggy green again.

Whiteman was brave in WA's run chase, but he simply lacked the support needed.

Jack Nisbet snared 3-47 for NSW, including the key scalp of Whiteman in the 46th over, while Bryce Jackson chipped in with 2-58.

One rare highlight for WA came earlier in the day when Agar leapt high into the air to pull off a stunning one-handed catch at backward point to remove Ben Dwarshuis for 20.

title: 1,000 native trees planted to turn school playground into tiny forest
text:
Armed with wide-brimmed hats and child-sized gardening gloves, year 4 students on the NSW Far South Coast are swapping schoolbooks for tree saplings in a bid to boost biodiversity in their playground.

Students from St Peter's Anglican College at Broulee have spent the past week transforming a barren patch of their playground into what will become a self-sustaining microforest, to create a cooler, greener space.

Students have planted about 1,000 plants native to the region’s endangered coastal littoral rainforest. (ABC South East NSW: Mikayla McGuirk-Scolaro)

"We're trying to bring back some of those endangered species that were lost in the 2020 bushfires, which was really unfortunate for all of our native animals and plants," year 4 student Zale Neal said.

" It feels really calming to plant all these plants, and to know that when we get older, we can have a microforest and say to our kids we've done that. "

It is the first school in NSW to partner with not-for-profit organisation Microforest Collective to research, design and plant a microforest as part of the curriculum.

One-of-a-kind project

Microforests, or tiny forests, are dense patches of native vegetation planted in urban or degraded areas, often no bigger than a tennis court.

Microforest Collective co-founder and landscape architect Edwina Robinson said the project used a Japanese planting technique known as the Miyawaki method, which involved densely planting a mixture of local species to accelerate growth.

She said the method helped the plants grow up to 10 times faster than normal, with the microforest expected to reach about 7 metres in height within two to three years.

Edwina Robinson discovered the Miyawaki method after the 2019-2020 bushfires. (ABC South East NSW: Mikayla McGuirk-Scolaro)

"Forests take hundreds of years to develop, but with this method we're actually short circuiting a lot of that," Ms Robinson said.

The school project uses a water-harvesting system designed to overcome the site's sandy soil.

About 40 metres of underground trenches have been lined with clay to capture rainwater.

Microforest Collective raised $20,000 to create the Eurobodalla's first microforest at St John’s Anglican Church in Moruya. (ABC South East NSW: Mikayla McGuirk-Scolaro)

Ms Robinson said the aim was to create resilient green spaces that could also help communities respond to a changing climate.

"By careful plant selection and good improvement of the soil, we can really change our microclimate and we can start creating shade," she said.

Students followed the Miyawaki planting method, which involves densely planting a mixture of local species to accelerate growth. (ABC South East NSW: Mikayla McGuirk-Scolaro)

Hundreds of plants in the ground

Students, teachers and volunteers have spent the past week planting about 1,000 plants native to the region's endangered coastal littoral rainforest.

Year 4 teacher Danielle Phillips said the group visited local rainforests, identified species and researched the conditions different plants needed to survive, before picking up gardening gloves.

Danielle Phillips says the project incorporated subjects such as maths, science and geography. (ABC South East NSW: Mikayla McGuirk-Scolaro)

She said students then completed a site analysis before designing where plants should go using science, maths, geography and literacy.

"When we were looking at the area that we were going to plant, how big is the area? What are we going to do regarding the amount of mulch? OK, well, let's work out the volume," Ms Phillips said.

" These kids are learning social emotional skills out here. How they connect, how they communicate, how they work as a team, what happens when things get challenging. "

Students spent a week planting native trees, shrubs and climbing plants. (ABC South East NSW: Mikayla McGuirk-Scolaro)

Growing up beside the forest

The collective now plans to use the project as a model for other schools.

Chair Jo Abbott said members had worked with the school's teachers to develop design templates and programs.

Jo Abbott hopes the project will be replicated by other schools. (ABC South East NSW: Mikayla McGuirk-Scolaro)

"If a school decided to take on a forest, they would be able to pick up these ready-to-go curriculum programs and then implement them within their school environment," she said.

Although Ms Abbott had doubts about how the students would feel getting their hands dirty, she said she was surprised by how enthusiastically they had taken to it.

"They are kids that spend a lot of time in nature, and enjoy being out doing hard work," she said.

The students will grow up with the microforest as they progress through school. (ABC South East NSW: Mikayla McGuirk-Scolaro)

title: It's time to tell the truth of Australia's Chinese history
text:
This year's Boyer Lecture series explores the opportunities and challenges of Australia's engagement with Asia in the 21st century. Dr Louisa Lim, Associate Professor at the University of Melbourne, reported from China for a decade for NPR and the BBC. This is an edited extract of her lecture, Tell it Slant.

When I was asked to reflect on Australia's role as part of Asia, I sat on a flat, white beach under a grey winter sky and thought about what that meant.

I suspected I was meant to address the logic of political realignment; potential economic markets; durable bridges between Australia and Asia. Tidy bullet points, bolstered by neat statistics, tessellating into a clear argument. (Preferably one that would fit on an Instagram tile.) Instead, I'm going to talk about a dancing white lion… but not quite yet.

As the sky darkened over that beach, I felt the weight of being the first Asian Boyer lecturer. I'm a new Australian, one of just three years standing. I have a Singapore Chinese father, a white British mother. I've written two books about the Chinese Communist Party's erasure and rewriting of its own history. What do I know of Asia and Australia?

Dr Louisa Lim is a journalist, author and University of Melbourne lecturer. (Supplied: Laura Du Vé)

The topic needed research. My first stop was Readings in Carlton, in Melbourne's north, with its stock of tens of thousands of books. At the counter, a harried man was punching at the till.

When I asked if they had any books on Australia's Asian history, he seemed surprised. He said they used to have one.

We went over to the Australian Studies section together. Eighteen shelves, maybe 400 books. He ran his hand over the spines.

"It's not there, I'm afraid," he said, crestfallen.

"What was it?" I asked.

"A biography," he said. "Someone in Bendigo. I can't remember who."

After that, I asked the same question at every bookshop I went to. Each time, it was a no. Though my writing explores forgotten and hidden histories, I was surprised to glimpse that invisibility here in Australia.

To be fair, these books do exist; more than 40 titles on the history of Chinese in Australia have been published in the past decade, but none were on the shelves of the shops I visited. They're not mainstream. You would only find the canon of work if you know where to look (in work done by scholars like Mei-fen Kuo and Juanita Kwok).

But there isn't even a single university course on the subject, let alone an Asian Australian studies centre at an Australian university.

History is story is identity. And that continuing invisibility has deep consequences for Australia's Chinese population.

The costs we pay

"When I was six years old, one of the kids at school called me 'Ching Chong Chinaman, born in a jar, christened in a teapot'. Ha, ha, ha."

That's Photographer William Yang. He was born in Dimbulah in Queensland in 1943.

"I had no idea what he was talking about, although I knew from his expression he was being horrible to me. So I went home to my mother and I said to her, 'Mum, I'm not Chinese, am I?' And she said, 'Yes, you are.' Her tone was hard, and it shocked me. And I knew in that moment, that being Chinese was like a terrible curse."

William Yang and his family pictured at their home in Dimbulah in Far North Queensland in the 1950s. (Supplied: Sydney Festival)

I heard this story last year at William's show, named Milestone. It took me straight back to 2016. I was sitting in the principal's office of a state primary school. We'd just arrived in Melbourne.

My eight-year-old had complained they'd been teased by a boy, backed up by his mates. He'd been taunting them with "ching chang chong", pulling back his eyes. Yes, this was in 2016. The same old story as William's, but almost 70 years later.

I wanted to know what action the school would take. But the principal was a busy woman, with a school to run. She looked at me as if I were a naughty child.

"The boys were only joking," she said wearily. "They've been told not to do it. It won't happen again."

That day I discovered there were no teachers of colour at that school. There was no one who even recognised racism. And it's still common.

According to the 2023 recent Lowy Institute report on being Chinese in Australia, one in five Chinese Australians reported being called offensive names in the past 12 months. For younger people aged 18 to 29 the reported rates of racism were even higher.

After that, I moved my child to another school. One with an excellent Chinese immersion program, diverse students and teachers. Every day for three years, we drove there and back. Half an hour each way, twice a day. Twelve hundred hours over three years. That was just one cost we paid. Five months' worth of workdays.

Listen to the Boyer Lecture Series on ABC listen Featuring distinguished speakers from across Australia, Singapore and Indonesia, this year's Boyer Lecture series explores the opportunities and challenges of Australia's engagement with Asia in the 21st century.

I was at work earlier this year, when the same child rang me. They're 19 years old now. But that day, they were sobbing so hard I couldn't understand what they were trying to say.

It turns out, they'd been walking down the street, holding hands with their boyfriend, just round the corner from his house in inner north Melbourne. Suddenly, a complete stranger began screaming at the pair of them; she was shouting "Find yourself an Australian girl!"

I dropped everything and I drove to pick them up. When I got there, the pair were sitting by the side of the road, heads bowed into each other, dazed. How can I talk about Australia's role in Asia when I'm crouched in the gutter, hugging my child?

Words and names matter

"Growing up in Australia, I've always felt very disconnected from my heritage."

That's comedian Noah Szto. He's a doctor who also writes very funny stand-up. He has a white Australian mother, and a Chinese Australian father.

"If you'd asked me when I was a kid how I felt racially, I probably would have told you that as far as I was concerned, I was 100 per cent white but there just happened to be a Chinese man in my house sometimes."

I've thought about those words a lot. For Noah, they're personal. But they also sum up the mindset left behind by the White Australia policy. Deep down, I suspect many Australians feel like Noah felt about his family: Australia is a white country that just happens to have Chinese people living in it.

That feeling is grounded in history. One reason for Federation, back in 1901, was to pass unified legislation limiting Chinese immigration. The modern Australian nation is rooted in anti-Chinese sentiment and in fear. When MPs debated the Federation bill, they were deciding not just who would be let into Australia, but who would be allowed to become Australian.

Being Chinese often precluded becoming Australian. The underlying fear, the anti-Chinese sentiment, they're still visible.

The boldness Australia needs has no political home right now When the Cold War ended, the US became Asia's uncontested leader. The hope, at the time, was that China would simply go along with that arrangement. Clearly, that's not how things are turning out.

One school holidays, I took my family to Bright, in Victoria's High Country. It was bitterly cold. We went sledding, whooping as we skidded down the white hills, our cheeks chapped by snow. The next day I got up early to visit the Chinese bridge at Wandiligong. It marks the contributions of the Chinese miners who transformed a small village into the largest town in the region in the 1850s.

Nowadays the Chinese bridge is handsome, painted red, crowned at either end with a corrugated iron pagoda. I was pleased to see Chinese contributions so publicly remembered. Then I read the signboards. They quoted books of the time. This was how they described Chinese miners: "To us they were just chows or chinks to be ridiculed and baited or given a wide berth."

Those words felt like a slap in the face.

Another year, our holiday trip was to Metung, in East Gippsland. My morning run skirted the beautiful bayside, taking me through a place called Chinaman's Creek. That word stopped me short. Chinaman. According to the Macquarie dictionary, it's "widely considered to be an offensive term". Yet there are still 235 places in Australia with 'Chinaman' or 'Chinamen' in their names. It's just one indication of how normalised anti-Chinese racism still is in Australian life.

Names matter. As the author Richard Flanagan said, "We become the words we speak." This repetition and incantation of racism, it replicates and amplifies it.

A scattered history

After that, I began seeking out Australian Chinese history. I needed other narratives, ones that were more useful to me.

That was why I was tramping up a hill in Vaughan, south of the central Victorian town of Castlemaine, with my friend Natasha. Our feet rustled through the copper-coloured gum leaves. We knew we were in the right place when we found stones arrayed in a perfect circle on the ground.

This was the Chinese cemetery from the mid-1850s, at the peak of the gold rush, when there were 49,000 Chinese immigrants on the Victorian goldfields. They had to pay entry taxes of 10 pounds a head, about $15,000 today; they also paid residence taxes not imposed on any other group.

"Daylesford Cemetery: on the Daylesford-Trentham road, 1.5km east of the Farmers Arms Hotel, across the street from the Daylesford Dharma school, one Chinese headstone: severe damage."

This is the poetry of Grace Yee, from her collection Joss: A History. Grace spent two years in the State Library of Victoria. She read the archives, then she turned them into poetry. Even the Bulletin's Anti-Chinaman Special Number of 1888.

By then, anti-Chinese sentiment had led to organised attacks on Chinese in Buckland, in Lambing Flats, mob violence in Bendigo, Ballarat, Maryborough and elsewhere.

Natasha and I used Grace's poetry as our guidebook; we couldn't find any other.

"Maryborough Cemetery: on the outskirts of town, a 17 minute walk south-east from the Maryborough Wattle Reserve Netball complex, eighteen Chinese headstones: gardeners, labourers, storekeepers: humble lane. From 2.8km west of Ballarat Bird world."

The poetry provided unexpected compass points, orienting us differently to landscape and history. Headstones whose Chinese calligraphy was worn smooth by wind and rain. A brick tower for burning paper offerings.

The sights we were seeing felt strangely archaeological. Holes in the ground that had once been Chinese baths. A Mad Max moonscape. Once, a Chinese mine, now dotted with burned-out cars.

"Chiltern cemetery, 1.3km northeast… near the Chiltern bushland reserve. Four Chinese graves, friends meeting)."

But this is recent history, just 170 years old. The visible traces of Chinese migrants on the landscape are so clear, yet so much of Australia's Chinese heritage is now lost. Forgotten, abandoned. Victim to the 20th-century racism of white Australia.

What remains of our Chinese history lies scattered, but the connective tissue is missing.

Poet Grace Yee won the 2024 Victorian Prize for Literature for her verse novel, Chinese Fish. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

These gaps are being filled by the poets and artists, the photographers and novelists. Maybe the artists are less governed by institutions, less governable. Those institutions have gate-kept the past, deciding what research to fund, what to teach, what Australian students should learn. The Roman empire, oh yes. Australia's Asian history, less so.

The poets and artists, the photographers and novelists; they're freer agents. Their work is freighted, weighted, fuelled by white hot anger, burning curiosity, the need to explore the gaps in their own histories.

They have family trees that go back a single generation. Grandfathers who changed their names, wiping clean their Asian pasts, internalising that racism into the silence that became a family legacy.

Again, I think of a poet's words — Emily Dickinson this time: "Tell all the truth but tell it slant."

That word "slant" is so tainted by racism and the taunts of the playground… but it's time to reclaim it.

Emily Dickinson writes, "Success in circuit lies", and maybe the circuitous route journeys through photographers' eyes, poets' words, to reach a different set of truths about Australia's past. Both about the extent of Chinese influence in Australia, and the ugliness of the persecution.

"Let's languish on Little Bourke street; the longest continuous/Chinese settlement in the western world."

Back in 1968, in his Boyer lectures, the anthropologist WEH Stanner coined the term The Great Australian Silence. The cult of forgetfulness, as he put it, practised on a national scale towards Indigenous people and history.

The lie of the tabula rasa wipes out 65,000 years of First Nations history. That Great Australian Silence has over time swallowed up Australia's Chinese history too; we need to fill it with voices, lives, stories.

"I am learning to/Prioritise my heritage in this shiny-buckled civilisation, /Where yellow-perilled white men brass the city's walls."

History is story is identity

When I moved here, I felt more Chinese than I ever have. Maybe because that was the way I was treated.

It came as a surprise that so many Australians seemed to view the country as part of Europe, just displaced to the other side of the world. As historian David Walker writes, Australia has seen itself as "a nation in the region but not of it".

That mental geography needs to change. Our future is here as part of Asia.

And so too is our past. History is story is identity.

It is an indisputable fact that some of Australia's cities were also Chinese cities. For four decades, Darwin had more Chinese residents than white ones. Broome's population was majority Asian for much of the first half of the 20th century. Bendigo's population was 20 per cent Chinese. Many Indigenous people also have Chinese heritage.

Loong during the 1910 Easter procession in Bendigo. (Supplied: Golden Dragon Museum/Vincent Kelly )

Australia has never been a monoculture. Its history is not a singular narrative. It is polyphonous, multilingual, plural. Yet the country keeps looping back into the same stale old arguments, driven by domestic politics.

That disregard for Australia's Asian history has dire consequences in the present, most urgently a lack of Asia capacity.

My child was very lucky to go to a Chinese immersion school. Only seven government schools offer Chinese immersion programmes in the whole of Australia. Just four secondary schools. (Only three per cent of our high school students learn Chinese, Japanese or Indonesian.)

Fewer than five students a year graduate from honours programmes in Chinese studies with language skills. We can barely talk to our neighbours, let alone understand them.

We need different role models, new points of reference.

I found one a few years ago when I was invited to the Bendigo Writers festival. I was speaking at the Golden Dragon Museum. When I walked inside, I was astonished to find myself face to face with a gigantic dragon. His head alone, fringed with blue gills, was bigger than my whole body. This is Dai Gum Loong, the longest processional dragon in the world.

He's the highlight of Bendigo's Easter parade. After I saw him, I went back the next year with my family.

It was a true community event. Stilt walkers led the parade, followed by BMX bikers, firefighters, religious puppets.

How to build a dragon Two of Bendigo's Golden Dragons were vandalised earlier this year. In the wake of the heartbreak, we tell the story of the third dragon.

And dragons of literally every stripe. From all over Australia. There was a Falun gong dragon carried by members of a sect banned in China. There was a LGBTQIA+ dragon in trans colours.

And, of course, there was Dai Gum Loong.

Longer than a soccer pitch, carried by more than sixty Bendigonians, of all ethnicities, all genders.

The thing is: dragon dances at Easter aren't a Chinese tradition at all. It's one that began in Bendigo in 1892. In the Golden Dragon museum, I saw sepia pictures of the people responsible. Chinese men with white wives and Wasian kids. Families like mine, but a century and a half earlier. They stayed on through the White Australia era, and they used their traditions to raise money for Bendigo's hospital.

This dragon, and the museum itself, they were both the brainchild of Russell Goldfield Jack. An Australian born in 1935, he's also known as Louey Yeung Man. He was the subject of the book I couldn't find at Readings, a biography by Dianne Dempsey.

Sadly, he has just passed away, aged 91.

Jacinta Allan and Russell Jack. (Supplied: Facebook)

In September I went to his funeral. He was accompanied on his last journey by a silver-white funeral lion, the Chinese colour of mourning. It shimmered as it danced slowly through Bendigo's streets.

In the theatre where his funeral was held, the lion bowed to his coffin, which was covered with an Australian flag. This was the first ever state funeral for a Chinese Australian.

"He was a great man, a great Australian," said former state premier Jacinta Allan.

At the grave side, people bowed with incense. His family burned paper money. The funeral lion went up in flames too, as firecrackers exploded around us.

I never met Russell Jack, but I benefited from his legacy. He made visible a different version of Australia's history. One that foregrounds Australia's Asian history, its Asian story, its Asian identity.

The white lion is the symbol of a society where citizens do not need to choose between being Australian and being Asian. To truly integrate into the region, Australia first needs to reckon with its own Asian past, and its continuing legacy of racism.

Story is history is identity. But this time, let's tell it slant.

This lecture and other Boyer Lectures will air on consecutive Sundays from October 18 on ABC Radio National's Sunday Extra program. They can also be found on ABC listen.

title: Valkyries shut down Borlase's Dream to square WNBA Finals
text:
Gabby Williams scored 17 points on Saturday (Sunday AEST) to help the visiting Golden State Valkyries post a 67-62 victory over the Atlanta Dream and even the WNBA Finals at two games apiece.

Tiffany Hayes and Veronica Burton each scored 13 points for Golden State, which won despite making just four of its 25 3-point attempts. Cecilia Zandalasini had 10 points and Kiah Stokes pulled down 16 rebounds for the Valkyries, who return home for Game 5 ‌on Monday.

Rhyne Howard led Atlanta with 19 points while Jordin Canada and Australia's Izzy Borlase chipped in 10 apiece. Angel Reese (eight points) and Allisha Gray (five points) shot a combined 3-for-19 from the field.

Atlanta sliced its 16-point ‌half-time deficit to 46-40 when Borlase made a 3-pointer with 4:27 left in the third ⁠quarter.

title: Regional students band together for unique performance
text:
For instrumental music students in regional and remote areas, the opportunities to practice their craft with a full ensemble can be few and far between.

However, a group of music teachers in rural South Australia has found a way to make it happen.

Music students from 14 schools across the Mid North and Southern Flinders Ranges have converged at the Peterborough Town Hall for an annual concert with members of the Adelaide Youth Orchestra (AYO).

The first iteration in 2023 saw 50 students performing.

This year, there were 100.

Students practised the songs all year before coming together for the concert. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

For some it was their first time playing as part of an ensemble of that scale, with most of them honing their craft in remote classrooms.

The concert is the brainchild of music teacher Kate Mawson, who previously taught instrumental music online to students at nine different schools in the region.

“Learning instruments in such a remote way, what better way to come with a common interest in one central location,” Ms Mawson said.

Striking a chord

Ms Mawson said music was a hard subject to translate online, but she made it work with some "creative ways of communicating".

"I would put colourful dots on their instruments and say, 'You need to press the red dot or the pink dot,'" she said.

Kate Mawson is the music teacher who spearheaded the performance. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

For the first time in a few years, students at Orroroo Area School have had access to in-person music lessons this year.

Student Lucas Wood said it made learning trumpet much easier.

"[Online is] a bit trickier than in person because trumpets are pretty loud, so sometimes it doesn't cross through but it's still fun," Lucas said.

Lucas Wood (left) and Toby Nutt used to have their trumpet lessons online. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

This year he had a solo at the concert.

"I can be a bit nervous, but I've been doing it for a while so it's not that bad," he said.

" It feels really good playing with all the different kinds of instruments. It's a lot different to just trumpets. "

Another student performer, Toby Nutt, "sometimes" practices his trumpet at home, to varying reactions from his family.

"They say I have to be in a different room every time I practice," he said.

This was his second year taking part in the concert.

"It's not too bad since there's so many instruments, if you mess up you can't really be heard," he said.

Taking centre stage

Orroroo Area School is one of several that have access to in-person instrumental music education again this year, through the Department for Education's Instrumental Music program.

"There was a period where we couldn't staff it at all … It was only the end of last year that we found two in-person staff to actually deliver weekly lessons," program leader David Hopgood said.

The program brings music teachers to schools across regional South Australia for weekly classes, but only once a year are they all in the same room.

"They play together at their school, and then they come here and they've got a huge room full of peers who are doing the same thing as they are, so that's really important," Mr Hopgood said.

David Hopgood leads the Instrumental Music program. (ABC Rural: Isabella Kelly)

The concert also gives students the chance to see the Adelaide Youth Orchestra at work.

"We talk about pathways, which is, you take up an instrument … where does it go?" Mr Hopgood said.

"If you just have the joy of playing the instrument, that's fine as well, but also going into an ensemble is so important. We really believe in that."

More than 130,000 degree-qualified jobs could be wiped out by AI within a decade, a sobering government report by the agency tasked with assessing the nation’s future skills has warned. Jobs and Skills Australia has forecast “around 139,000” fewer jobs requiring a university degree in 10 years, with four of the top 10 occupations for graduates of commerce/management and society and culture at “medium risk” of automation. Trades jobs are expected to peak in the coming decade as degree-qualified roles decline. Matthew Absalom-Wong Futurist Michael McQueen said studying the humanities or forgoing university for a trade will give people entering the workforce an advantage over those in “highly cognitive but repetitive roles”. Essential to future-proofing is letting go of the idea of “university as the ultimate and the ideal” and giving vocational jobs equal consideration, McQueen said. “It’s no longer a sensible paradigm.”

Advertisement

Within universities, the critical thinking and creativity engendered by arts degrees make them a good option, he said. “It’s a way of thinking more than the actual skills that you’re learning,” he said, cautioning against going to university “because it’s the right thing to do”. The JSA analysis earlier this month shows jobs that are popular with university graduates are among those at risk. Accounting and financial services (management and commerce), admin and HR (management and commerce), admin and HR (society and culture) and legal and insurance (society and culture) are among the top five occupations for graduates of both disciplines. They have also been deemed at medium risk of “complete displacement” from AI automation.

Advertisement

Management and commerce graduates’ other top occupational choices – advertising/media, sales and executive roles – have been rated at a low risk of AI replacement. For society and culture graduates, top occupations with a low risk of AI replacement include health, education and advertising/media. But a number of those occupations are rated as high risk of AI taking over some elements of the industry. Jobs and Skills’ acting commissioner Trevor Gauld said: “The future is not fixed.” “It is true that entry-level roles may have some exposure challenges. But what we know is that human judgment, expertise and adaptability remains crucial. You gain many of those skills through those entry-level pathways. So this is about choice. If we don’t choose to ensure that we maintain those entry-level roles, how will the next generation of workers develop those judgment skills?”

Advertisement

Advertisement

“When you look at the priorities in this nation right now, we’re talking about housing, we’re talking about the care economy,” he said. “We’re talking about a future made in Australia. Huge numbers of these roles require an apprenticeship or traineeship pathway. There is huge opportunity for really meaningful, well-remunerated work in a whole range of occupations with quite low exposure. “But even those occupations with higher exposure, we still need that human judgment, we still need that critical thinking.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. text:

BusinessCompaniesWestern Sydney International ‘Final piece of the puzzle’: Western Sydney Airport opens for business Chris Zappone Updated October 25, 2026 — 1:40pm ,first published October 25, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
