The first commercial flight from Sydney’s – and Australia’s – newest international airport took off this morning from Western Sydney International bound for the Gold Coast. Flight JQ362, with 188 passengers, aviation enthusiasts and journalists on board, departed at 11.22am. Thirty places were reserved for Jetstar officials and journalists and the rest for the paying public. As it taxied on the lone runway in the late morning light, crowds of plane spotters jammed nearby hillsides to get a glimpse of history. A helicopter hovered nearby. The flight was filled with passengers wearing Jetstar and WSI hats, aviation super-fans, proud western Sydneysiders and the generally curious. After a flight of one hour and nine minutes, JQ362 landed at its destination.

Advertisement

George Rasho was proud to be on the first flight from the new airport. The Age On the flight, western Sydney-based businessman George Rasho said he specifically booked to be on the inaugural journey. It was important to Rasho because WSI represented demographics of western Sydney. “It feels like the government has heard our voices, giving us the privilege of having a nearby airport,” said Rasho. “I’m proud to know that we are now put on the map for the world – and for the world to see one of the most multicultural places on Earth [in western Sydney].”

Advertisement

The federal government, which has backed the airport, and the City of Sydney hope WSI will give travellers a new option with round-the-clock, curfew-free flights domestically and internationally. Qantas-owned Jetstar is also vying to fly from WSI to Bali. The low-cost carrier is flying Airbus A320s, which seats up to 188 passengers, forming part of Jetstar’s newer, more-efficient and easier-to-operate fleet. Loading Before the first flight, passengers expressed excitement, relief and a little curiosity about being on the historic journey. Madi Merc, who lives near the airport, booked places for herself and her three children.

Advertisement

“Being on the flight is everything,” she said. “I was nine years old when I moved to Australia.” “I grew up on the farms around us,” said Merc, who said she’s trained for half Ironman contests and participated in the runway run before the airport was open. “To fly out of here now feels like the final piece of the puzzle,” she said. “It’s absolutely wild to say that where cows and sheep once grazed, there’s now people flying around. It’s really cool.” Moreover, Merc said she faced a 20-minute drive to the airport instead of an hour.

Advertisement

Jetstar expects to fly up to 24 return services a week from WSI. That means up to 14 a week to Melbourne, daily services to the Gold Coast and three weekly to Brisbane. Related Article Aviation Wheels up for Australia’s newest major airport as first flight takes off The addition of WSI as a new point of demand within Australia’s network of airports was overshadowed by a sense of relief by passengers who milled around the lobby before tagging luggage and going through security to the gate. The airport’s clean, well-lighted space played host to a low-key celebratory atmosphere with T-shirts, press conferences and mascot. The day began with a First Nation’s smoking ceremony, and the sense of place was evident in the design and layout of the facility. As passengers boarded, Australia’s political class – past and present – gathered and spoke in a nearby gate. Speakers including Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and NSW Premier Chris Minns, but the crowded was also filled with figures who’d help realise the project of the airport.

Advertisement

Aviation influencer Julian Tseng flew from Melbourne and was able to claim the first seat on the first domestic flight. The inaugural flight at the brand new Western Sydney International Airport takes off as dignitaries watch. Audrey Richardson Tseng, who describes himself as a “bit of a geek”, said: “It’s a historical occasion, not just for Sydney but for all of Australia. It’s not every day you get to witness the opening of a new airport.” Jetstar CEO Steph Tully championed the airline’s role in bringing “more choice and low fares to western Sydney”. “This is an historic day for aviation in Australia,” she said.

Advertisement

“We’ve got a strong track record of opening up new markets, and western Sydney, one of the fastest growing regions in the country, is going to be one of the great ones.” The initial route map is fairly modest to start, but it should expand over time as WSI settles in alongside Kingsford Smith. Related Article Airports ‘Slow burn’: Western Sydney Airport’s real challenge awaits after launch Eventually, WSI looks set to cater mostly to budget and leisure travel, while Kingsford Smith remains the main hub for premium and business trips. To mark the start of flights from WSI and induce passengers to try the airport, Jetstar announced fare sales featuring WSI-Gold Coast one-way fares starting from $54, WSI-Melbourne from $61 and WSI-Brisbane from $65.

Advertisement

But with a new airport come new baggage rules for passengers. The one-way fares will feature Jetstar’s new policy in which every passenger receives an under-seat personal item and access to overhead bins incurs an additional fee. Those who purchase bin access will board the plane first. The first international service takes place on Monday when Air New Zealand operates its inaugural flights connecting WSI and Auckland. In keeping with the leisure focus of WSI, Fiji Airways will fly three times a week starting in March. Additionally, passengers from WSI will be able to fly to Singapore with Singapore Airlines in November, and to Ho Chi Minh City with VietJet early next year.

Advertisement

At the end of next year, Virgin partner Qatar Airways will fly three return services a week to Doha. VietJet also plans to add direct Bangkok services by November next year, pending regulatory approval. Qantas will operate eight flights a week to Brisbane and Melbourne beginning next year. Key points DANCE: The Australian Ballet return to the State Theatre with The Nutcracker

MUSIC: Louis Tomlinson puts on a big show at John Cain Arena

DANCE

The Nutcracker ★★★★

The Australian Ballet, Ian Potter State Theatre, Arts Centre Melbourne, until October 31 The State Theatre has reopened after 2½ years of renovations, and Arts Centre Melbourne is keen to reassure audiences that its familiar character survives. The Australian Ballet has taken the hint, returning home with Peter Wright’s The Nutcracker, created for Birmingham Royal Ballet in 1990: an old favourite offering reassurance on a suitably extravagant scale. Yuumi Yamada as Clara in The Nutcracker. Kate Longley John F. Macfarlane’s gigantic, dreamy designs seem almost to have grown out of the theatre. The Stahlbaums’ drawing room, swathed in dark red curtains, extends the auditorium’s crimson plush into the family Christmas party. With festive decorations glistering like seams of emerald in the shadows, the whole experience feels deliciously subterranean: a theatre and a household tucked into the same deep burrow. We’re all here underground together. Yuumi Yamada supplies the youthful enthusiasm this cosy fantasy needs. Her Clara, a ballet student dreaming herself into a ballerina, is eager, unguarded and winsomely adolescent, and her delight in everything has an attractive freedom. Jarryd Madden’s fatherly Drosselmeyer offers a steadying presence.

Advertisement

The finest enchantment in this version remains Wright’s reimagined version of the Dance of the Snowflakes at the end of the first act, led here by Isobelle Dashwood’s graceful Snow Fairy. On Saturday night, the second act sometimes felt rushed. The national dances were briskly dispatched, and the Waltz of the Flowers grew a little unruly, the ensemble’s lines scattering beneath Macfarlane’s overhead tangle of streamers. Intentional or otherwise, the visual rhyme was actually quite enjoyable: the flowers and their consorts seemed to have caught the delirium of the decoration. But the entrance of Sharni Spencer’s queenly Sugar Plum Fairy soon restored order. The battle beneath the Christmas tree impresses. Kate Longley The theatre itself still smells new. The seats are a considerable improvement, although the space between rows feels even more miserly than before. The additional aisles do, however, offer more accessibility. The gridlock in the stalls after the curtain comes down is now, I hope, a thing of the past. The acoustics require a more cautious verdict after one visit, but, still, Orchestra Victoria – led by Jonathan Lo – sounded very good to me, with a notably crisp brass section. Familiarity has its attractions and there is still plenty in this production – such as the battle beneath the Christmas tree – that impresses. On the other hand, after nearly two decades and five seasons in The Australian Ballet’s repertoire, this Nutcracker is starting to feel a little old-fashioned. The building has had its renovation – now for the ballet?

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann

Advertisement

MUSIC

Louis Tomlinson ★★★★

John Cain Arena, October 20 The screams that greet Louis Tomlinson give me a contact high. Die-hard fans have legged it to the barrier and thrust stage. The word “Lemonade” flashes on-screen, towering over Tomlinson and his five-piece band. He cuts an amiable, Gallagher-type figure in a puffy red jacket and jeans. Until he’s briefly engulfed in a confetti explosion. Louis Tomlinson performing at John Cain Arena on October 20. Richard Clifford Music videos are composed live, faces projected dystopia-large with film effects, high-contrast overlays or psychedelic sunflowers, with colour-saturated stage lights and even a synth-laser show for Broken Bones. It’s a leap from the opening act, Rum Jungle, the kind of Aussie indie group you play driving to the beach on P-plates with your mates.

Advertisement

Tomlinson gets somewhat swallowed in the production. The mixing does no favours, his piping, Arctic Monkeys-style vocals no match for thundering drums in songs like The Spark. He’s often lost in backing harmonies and the word-faithful crowd, unless it’s the pared-back cover of the Foo Fighters’ My Hero. But Tomlinson’s impeccable band shines. Oozing rock, they unify eclectic leaps from funk pop and acoustic ballads to nostalgic indie/Britpop like the Oasis-esque Saturdays and Franz Ferdinand-style dance riffs in Out of my System. Keyboard skips between plinking piano and glimmering synth as the guitarists and bassist pace like tigers to tumbling, chest-shaking beats and rip blistering solos. The word “Lemonade” flashes on-screen over Tomlinson and his five-piece band. Richard Clifford Tomlinson performs a pop persona perfectly. Gracious and grateful. Hand on heart, pointing to swooning fans. His grinning, Yorkshire-accented commentary is lightly peppered with profanities: “Loud as you fooken’ can!” In return, the One Direction star is utterly adored. For One Direction’s Night Changes, a sea of phones rise, recording intently. Tomlinson’s grim-faced guards have to pull him back from the barrier when ladies get grabby in the encore. I only wonder if he regretted the jacket in the fervent, feminine body heat filling John Cain Arena.

title: Big W has spent more than a decade in Kmart’s shadow. Can it pull off a comeback?
text:

Mother-of-two Jun Bei Liu visited Kmart just last week. Her trip to Kmart Chatswood Chase yielded new lunch boxes for the kids, organisational baskets and decorative trays, to go with some recently purchased Anko vases. Her 13-year-old son and his friend also paid a visit to the Sydney store. “They bought a pair of slides,” she said. “It’s the first time they’ve ever been to the shops by themselves.” Liu is lead portfolio manager of Ten Cap, which handles funds exceeding $1.6 billion and is invested in Kmart’s parent company, Wesfarmers, but not Woolworths, Big W’s owner. By contrast, her last visit to Big W was about seven years ago. She remembers the department store in Macquarie Centre as having a messy apparel section, harsh lighting with a “warehouse feel”, a limited homewares section, and is not in a hurry to revisit. “If I have to travel far and wide to find this store when it’s not convenient, and it doesn’t provide all the categories I need, why should I go there?” Big W’s sticky narrative as Australia’s runner-up discount chain is unfortunately yet inevitably defined by how it is dwarfed by its more impressive, domineering rival Kmart, which for more than a decade has cemented its crown as the nation’s preferred discount department store. Today, Big W’s national footprint (178 stores) is about half the size of Kmart’s (more than 300), after 30 store closures were announced in 2019. While Kmart consistently produces more than $1 billion in profits, Big W’s have been in a downward slide for several years, and sank to minus $33 million in the 2025 financial year.

Advertisement

Some wonder what parent company Woolworths intends to do with it. In early 2025, the supermarket group’s chief executive, Amanda Bardwell, reignited speculation that a sale or exit of Big W might be on the cards after announcing a strategic review of the “shape of its business portfolio”. Management are eager to impart that a corner has been turned. Big W swung back into the black in the latest financial year, turning a $64 million profit thanks to less heavy discounting, stronger clothing sales and a thriving marketplace business. “We’re still early days in our transformation,” said Big W managing director Dan Hake. “We’ve had an important milestone this financial year, which was to prove out that we can step up our game in product. We can be absolutely competitive on price, and we can be lean and consistent enough in our operations that we can still make a profit at the end of the year. That’s just step one.” Big W managing director Dan Hake is overseeing the discount department store’s turnaround. Audrey Richardson The turnaround strategy is simple: keep shelf prices low, put better-quality products on the shelf, and get more efficient. Big W’s traditional areas of strength (“the purpose of Big W is to make a real difference for families,” said Hake) have been primarily in its kids’ offering, a books department so formidable that local book store operators complain it undercuts their market share, and toy aisles full of Barbies, Lego sets, Pokémon cards and Bluey merch.

Advertisement

Much investment has been poured into clothing, health and beauty, and homewares departments. Change rooms at newly renovated stores are painted in colourful pastels and large enough to fit prams. “We know that families spend on their kids first,” said Hake. “But we also want mum to have a great experience.” Store layouts are being reconfigured and trialled. Big W’s Plumpton store, 45 kilometres west of Sydney CBD, is among a handful of newly renovated stores with semi-enclosed sections for beauty and tech that are as much about driving people to explore what’s on the shelf as it is about stemming theft. In apparel, some price points are in the single digits (children’s tees for $3). A budget version of the popular barrel leg-style jeans sells for $30. About 80 per cent of the womenswear range is now under $20. “We’re not famous for it yet, but I think there’s great value,” said Hake. “We will get the growth, and we will become more front of mind for customers.” Big W Plumpton has been renovated to carve out distinct sections for health and beauty and tech products. Audrey Richardson Big W’s inescapable challenge is that it is stuck playing catch-up to Kmart, which has turned its in-house brand Anko into a standalone brand. But Big W cannot replicate Kmart’s strategy of turning private label products into 85 per cent of sales; it must juggle the dual task of growing exclusive-label lines without cannabilising its role as a “house of brands”. Kmart has organised its business around a tight supply chain that takes globally trending designs, bulk-ordering from Asian manufacturers in huge quantities, and selling them in Australia en masse. Its homewares and furniture department is so successful it has spawned an IKEA-like spin-off, K Home.

Advertisement

Shoppers on a budget, who have more price comparison tools today than ever, are choosing where to spend with ruthlessness. “If you’ve got a product and that product is even 10¢ cheaper at the competitor next door, that’s where they’re going to shop it. If quality is just a little bit off, and you’re trying to get away with saving costs in the wrong places, your customer is going to shop that product elsewhere,” said Hake. “These sound like little things, but to do it effectively at scale across the entire store, across all these different categories, it’s a big ask, right? You need to be absolutely on the ball.” It has demanded a broader cultural change across the organisation and a sharper focus on one united vision (“we are a price fighter on behalf of our customers”). More product designers and category managers have been brought in-house. “It’s a game of simplicity, stock flow, and just getting the basics right,” said Hake. Big W Plumpton is one of a handful of stores that have been renovated to entice shoppers. Audrey Richardson Where is Big W going? Big W’s position as runner-up goes deeper than mere numbers. Through Anko, Kmart’s offer to customers is unambiguous: designer-inspired products at budget prices. A loyal army of evangelists, in Facebook groups like Kmart Mums Australia or Kmart Home Decor & Hacks Australia, swap DIY hacks, styling tips and stock alerts with each other. “Kmart had a big hand in eliminating the bargain stigma, making it cool to shop there,” said RMIT University associate professor of marketing Dr Marian Makkar, pointing to “late night Kmart runs” becoming a social activity for teens and young adults.

Advertisement

Positioned as a “luxe-for-less” retailer, Kmart has gained cachet with Gen Z by delivering on style and aesthetic without the barrier of a high price tag, removing buyer’s remorse and increasing basket sizes, says Macquarie Business School marketing professor Jana Bowden. “That brand love for Kmart is the X factor,” said Bowden. “It’s what makes it different from its competitors. Kmart doesn’t just sell homewares and clothing. It sells a value consciousness, identity and a cultural moment.” It’s not clear how much time Hake has to execute Big W’s big turnaround. Rumours about the chain’s future have simmered for years. In August 2025, Bardwell announced Big W’s technology systems would be separated from Woolworths, a move often interpreted as preparing a business for potential demerging. Liu wonders if the market is big enough to accommodate many discount chains. Canadian giant Dollarama, which bought The Reject Shop early last year and is rebranding stores, runs a successful private label model that could threaten Kmart. “I really don’t know what that brand stands for, Big W,” Liu said. While a turnaround costs time and money, “how patient is Woolworths?” she asked. “You have to give it at least three years. I’m just not sure if Woolworths is that committed for [Big W] to turn around.” At Big W, Christmas began in September. Audrey Richardson

At 11.22am, a Jetstar aircraft soared into blue skies from Western Sydney International Airport, marking the start of passenger flights and a new era for both Sydney and the country. Looking on from the departure gates at flight JQ362 bound for the Gold Coast were hundreds of guests, many of whom played a key role in the development of Australia’s first major new airport in half a century. Jetstar flight JQ362 on the tarmac moments before it is pushed back for the first flight. Audrey Richardson Moments earlier, from the departures area looking out to the Blue Mountains, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese officially marked the opening by unveiling a commemorative plaque and paying tribute to those who had played a part. “Everyone who has been part of this story along the way can feel proud today. It has been a long and remarkable journey for all of us,” he said.

Advertisement

Albanese said that the city had looked to the harbour and the CBD for too long, and the new $6 billion airport would turn that around to where people lived and worked in western Sydney. On Jetstar flight JQ362 was Gold Coast resident Mark Ignativ, 54, who was the first to check in physically in the terminal. “It’s rarer than a solar eclipse to be on the first flight from a new airport. It’s pretty unusual, especially in Australia,” he said. “I’ve been here when it’s only farms and houses. Now it’s finally open, it’s really a game changer. A city this size needs at least two airports.”

Advertisement

He admitted he was a “little bit” of an aviation enthusiast but “not the type that sit on ladders with telescopes”. He is heading back to western Sydney from the Gold Coast on the return Jetstar flight. Another on board was Hong Kong resident Jaing Liu, who flew to Sydney to join her daughter, TT Huang, to be part of history on the first flight. “This is a rare chance to be part of history. My mum is very excited,” said Huang, who lives in Sydney and describes herself as a plane enthusiast. TT Huang, left, and her mother, Jaing Liu, arrive at the airport to check in for the inaugural passenger flight. Audrey Richardson Flying the A320 out of the new airport were Jetstar captain Guy Proctor, 51, from the Gold Coast and first officer Aglaya Papadokokolakis, 25, from Blacktown.

“It’s definitely a privilege to have this opportunity. It’s a very special flight. To have the opportunity to fly out of an airport in my backyard is an amazing, amazing opportunity. It’s very special day,” Papadokokolakis said. The pilots are flying the return leg from the Gold Coast to the new airport. The inaugural passenger flight comes three months after cargo aircraft started flying to the curfew-free airport at Luddenham, on the city’s western fringe. Jetstar first officer Aglaya Papadokokolakis, 25, from Blacktown, and captain Guy Proctor, 51, from the Gold Coast outside the terminal. Audrey Richardson The airport is officially named after pioneering aviator Nancy-Bird Walton, known as the “Angel of the Outback”. It was fitting that among the guests was Walton’s daughter, Tweed, and the aviator’s granddaughters.

Western Sydney Airport chairman Paul O’Sullivan said the opening was the result of sustained conviction, adding that it had from benefited from bipartisan political support. “This is more than the opening of a building. It fulfils a nation-building promise to deliver a new 24-hour international gateway for Australia,” he said. “For decades, this airport existed only in the imagination of a small group of people with a bold vision. Today, that vision is a reality, and today is also evidence that Australia can deliver major infrastructure projects safely, on time and on budget.” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in the terminal on Sunday. Audrey Richardson Western Sydney Airport chief executive Simon Hickey said the airport was future-proofed and built to serve the city for the coming century. “When I think about that future, it’s genuinely difficult to fathom the impact Western Sydney International will have on greater Sydney,” he said.

Among guests were former prime ministers Tony Abbott and Scott Morrison, federal Labor ministers Chris Bowen, Don Farrell, Jason Clare and Michelle Rowland, as well as Premier Chris Minns and NSW governor-general Margaret Beazley. Abbott, who approved Badgerys Creek for the airport site in 2014, said it was his government that made the “final, irrevocable and definitive decision to make it happen”. A passenger in the check-in area before walking onto the first flight. Audrey Richardson Asked whether it would be a success, Abbott said it was likely to be a slow start before becoming the major airport for Sydney over the next 50 years due to its curfew-free status and growth in western parts. On Sunday, the airport also became a new tourist attraction as locals arrived to see the first flight, turning the terminal into a public space after years of largely being off limits during construction and fit-out.

Jetstar will operate up to 14 weekly flights between the new Commonwealth-owned airport and Melbourne, daily services to the Gold Coast, and three a week to Brisbane. Related Series

City life Welcome to Western Sydney International Airport Jetstar chief executive Stephanie Tully said taxis or Uber rides for people travelling to Sydney’s Kingsford Smith Airport were often the most expensive part of the journey. “For the people that live in this area, it’s just a massive step change to access and frequency and departures. This airport provides a choice for people in NSW, which they’ve never had before,” she said. “Our Gold Coast service we increased frequency before we even took off. title: 'Allegations of allegations': Greens senator takes leave amid misconduct investigation

In brief Jordon Steele-John says pressure over a misconduct probe has kept him out of parliament.

He denies wrongdoing and claims internal party politics are at play.

A Greens senator is taking leave from parliament, saying pressure surrounding a misconduct probe has left him "kept out by allegations of allegations".

Jordon Steele-John faces an independent investigation into several allegations surrounding inappropriate behaviour toward women between 2017 and 2025.

He has vehemently denied any wrongdoing.

The WA senator said he would heed a "growing chorus" opposing his appearing on Senate estimates committees next week.

"I have decided not to return next week and will instead focus on the independent and timely investigation I hope is soon commenced by the Greens WA," he said in a statement on Friday night.

title: 'You'll never forget the very first flight': How a new airport became a bucket-list item
text:
John Darcy had never set foot on a plane until he was 40.

Now, 18 years and 179 flights later, he'll be on the first international flight to leave Western Sydney International Airport.

The Sydney aviation enthusiast spent his childhood photographing planes and dreaming of travelling on one. On Monday morning, he'll board Air New Zealand flight NZ166 to Auckland, becoming one of the first international passengers to depart from Australia's newest airport.

"I started keeping account of my flights; it's become a hobby, collecting airports, collecting flight routes, collecting different types of planes flown on," Darcy told SBS News.

"I've flown 179 times, more than 60 airports in Australia, North America and Europe.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"But I needed to add Western Sydney International Airport to my tally."

Darcy is old enough to remember when the Hawke government announced Badgerys Creek as the site for Sydney's second airport.

Dubai from the air during one of Darcy's 179 flights. Source: Supplied

After decades of debate, delay and construction, he said it felt only right to be there from the start.

"It's been so long coming. To think that on Sunday, passengers will start flying in and out of there, and on Monday I will be on the first international flight out of there."

"It's for the little boy inside of me."

Sydney's second airport will welcome its first passengers this weekend, becoming Australia's first newly built international airport in more than 50 years.

Located near Badgerys Creek in western Sydney, the airport will initially host services from airlines including Jetstar, Qantas, Air New Zealand, Singapore Airlines, Fiji Airways, Qatar Airways and Vietjet.

Unlike Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport, flights can arrive and depart around the clock.

For aviation enthusiasts like Darcy, that makes the opening more than just an infrastructure project.

A few hours in Auckland

The destination, however, is almost beside the point.

Darcy will spend just one night in Auckland before flying home the following day.

"The only reason I'm doing this is for that inaugural flight," he said.

"I don't have any particular business in Auckland and I need to get back to resume work. I'm not taking holidays for this, just a couple of days off."

Four weeks later, he'll do something similar again, flying on Singapore Airlines' inaugural service from Western Sydney to Singapore.

"I'll be overnight in Auckland on Monday, but four weeks later when I go to Singapore, I'll be five hours in Changi Airport and then coming straight back."

"It's the novelty of the new airport and the badge of honour of being on the first international departure from that airport," he said.

There's also data behind that badge of honour.

Since 2014, he has logged every flight he can remember taking, tracking everything from flight numbers and aircraft types to which day of the week he travelled.

"It's on an Excel spreadsheet," he said.

"I've tracked all the data of the different flight sectors, the airlines, all the flight numbers, the length of all the flights, the departure airports, the arrival airports."

His trip from Western Sydney to Auckland has already been entered.

"It will be my 180th flight and 2,201 kilometres from Western Sydney to Auckland."

Darcy isn't the only aviation enthusiast making special plans for the airport's opening.

Some are buying tickets on inaugural flights. Others are heading to Sydney for a completely different view.

Chasing the perfect shot

For 19-year-old Alastair, the opening of Western Sydney International Airport is just as exciting. But while Darcy will be inside the plane, Alastair plans to be hundreds of metres away with a camera pointed at it.

The Melbourne plane spotter is flying to Sydney specifically to photograph the airport's first departures.

"I'm going up there to capture a moment in history because it's not every day that Australia gets a new international airport," he said. "It'll just be a once-in-a-lifetime thing."

Plane spotting, he explains, is about more than watching aircraft take off and land.

"It's like getting different plane liveries that normal people would see and think, 'Oh, that's just what a plane looks like'," he said.

"Sometimes there's a really special one, and it's very cool to see."

Plane spotter Alastair will be ready with a camera as the first flight takes off from Western Sydney International Airport. Source: Supplied

After discovering the hobby at 14, Alastair began keeping a notebook of every aircraft registration he spotted.

Five years on, that handwritten tally is closing in on 2,000 entries, and he now heads out plane spotting almost every day.

Sometimes that's at Melbourne Airport. Sometimes it's from a nearby park. Occasionally, it's from his own backyard.

What started with a phone camera has evolved into a serious setup worth about $5,000.

He uses flight-tracking apps to monitor aircraft movements and, when he's photographing at Melbourne Airport, often climbs ladders to shoot above the fence line.

Alastair uses ladders that can extend up to 6m to photograph planes above airport fence lines. Source: Supplied

"What we bring at Melbourne Airport are ladders," he said. "We bring ladders that can go three metres up so we can get a good shot above the fence line."

Fully extended, those ladders can reach 6m.

He's never fallen off one himself, although he's seen others take a tumble in pursuit of the perfect image.

The effort, he says, is worth it.

One of his favourite parts of the hobby is connecting with pilots, some of whom message him directly to ask for photos of their flights.

Pilots will sometimes acknowledge Alastair from the cockpit when he takes photos from the other side of the fence. Source: Supplied

"They'll wave from the cockpit or they'll do something to acknowledge me from the other side of the fence," he said.

"I think that's really cool."

A once-in-a-generation opening

Within Australia's plane spotting community, the opening of Western Sydney International Airport has become one of the most anticipated aviation events in years.

Alastair compares the excitement to the arrival of the Airbus A350-1000 ULR in Melbourne earlier this year, when aviation enthusiasts gathered to photograph the aircraft used during Qantas' record-breaking ultra-long-haul testing flights.

"I don't think anything will beat the hype of when the Airbus A350-1000 ULR came to Melbourne," he said.

"But the hype for Western Sydney, it's big.

"Everyone's excited to spot there. Everyone's excited to fly out of there. Everyone's excited to see what airlines will fly there."

Like Darcy, Alastair is interested in the history as much as the aircraft itself.

He's already hoping to capture a photo of the airport's first departures, particularly if one receives a ceremonial water-cannon salute.

But he says the real value of those images won't be obvious to everyone who sees them.

"It's like the backstory of the photos," he said.

"Someone's going to say, 'Oh, that's just a Jetstar plane taking off.'

"And I'd be like, 'No, that's the first passenger flight out of a new airport in so long in Australia.'

"You can always get a Jetstar A320 at Western Sydney in the next 20 years.

"But you'll never forget the very first flight."

title: Australians are having fewer babies. Can migration fill the gap?
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

"I had my baby at 38," says Heer Kaur, an Indian migrant living in Beveridge, north of Melbourne, who had always imagined having a big family.

But the reality of building a life in a new country, establishing a career and raising a child without family support meant rethinking that dream.

Kaur eventually decided to have just one child, weighing her desire for a large family against the financial and practical demands of parenthood.

"As migrants, we have to rebuild everything in the new country. I kept postponing marriage or having children for later. I wanted to be settled first. Be a permanent resident, build a career, have some stability," she tells SBS Punjabi.

"I wanted to have at least two kids. I assumed I would be able to have kids whenever I tried. But that was not the case."

SBS News has withheld her real name for privacy reasons.

Kaur says the lack of family support in Australia also meant spending more on childcare.

More money spent on childcare meant having to work longer to earn more, and then less time with my child. Then I had to settle for a quality life for my son, even though it meant him being an only child.

"The compromise comes with guilt as a parent. We work hard to ensure he learns social skills, how to share, and has a network of his own, beyond us."

She says she hopes the family she built was the result of her own choices, not dictated by social and economic circumstances.

Kaur's experience reflects a wider question facing Australia: what happens when the family people want, and the family they can afford, are not the same?

Previous Intergenerational Reports have predicted that Australia would have a higher fertility rate. Source: SBS News

Kaur is not alone in finding herself at this crossroads.

The Treasury's Intergenerational Report (IGR) 2026 puts Australia's total fertility rate at a historic low of 1.48 births per woman, lower than the total fertility rates projected in previous IGRs.

The replacement-level fertility rate — the rate at which a population replaces itself over time without migration — is about 2.1 births per woman.

The report projects that Australia's fertility rate will decline further to 1.34 births per woman by 2065–66.

It identifies delayed childbearing as a key factor contributing to smaller families and lower fertility rates.

Why are Australians delaying having kids?

The IGR identifies establishing a career as one reason people delay parenthood. It also points to access to childcare, the burden of unpaid care, housing security, and workplace flexibility as factors influencing people's decisions about whether to start a family or have more children.

The trend towards later childbearing is not unique to Australia.

In 2023, more than one in three births worldwide were to women aged 30 and over, compared with about one in four in 1990.

Source: SBS News

However, experts say delayed parenthood is only part of the picture. Financial pressures, changing social expectations and individual circumstances can also shape decisions about family size. The reasons vary, and lower fertility rates do not necessarily mean that everyone wants more children but is unable to have them.

But as Australia's fertility rate falls and its population ages, the implications extend beyond individual families.

The IGR warns that if birth rates and migration fall below baseline expectations, Australia's population would be 1.9 million smaller and the economy 7.4 per cent smaller by 2065–66.

And with deaths projected to outnumber births by the 2060s, migration is expected to play an increasingly important role in sustaining population growth and meeting workforce needs.

Australia's growing reliance on migration

Migrants already make up a large and growing share of the health care and social assistance workforce.

The IGR notes that migration can help moderate population ageing as new migrants are "typically younger than the existing population".

Source: SBS News

Demographer Liz Allen says Australia's ageing population and below-replacement fertility rate mean the country will rely more on migration to support its workforce and economy.

"Australia is on the way to what's considered super-aged. It essentially means that, in proportion speaking, we have more people aged over 65 than we have young people," she tells SBS Punjabi.

Demographer Liz Allen says Australia is moving towards becoming a super-aged society, meaning people aged 65 and over will make up a larger share of the population than younger Australians. Credit: Supplied

"Currently, we rely on individual income taxpayers to contribute to the economy; with an ageing population and below-replacement-level fertility, we have a shrinking relative working-age population. That means fewer tax dollars coming from that biggest source of taxpayers, individual workers."

At the moment, migrants present the biggest share of population growth in this country. And that's because the local population isn't growing the way it used to.

Allen says migration also brings social and cultural benefits alongside its economic contribution.

Source: SBS News

The IGR found new migrants are typically younger than the existing population, with a median age of 26 compared with 38 in 2024-25. As a result, migration helps slow population ageing and increases the share of working-age people beyond what would be achieved through natural increase alone.

Do migrants have more children?

Research by the University of Melbourne's demographer Peter McDonald shows that temporary migrants are predominantly young adults aged 20 to 35, many of whom come to Australia to study or establish their careers. While they are included in the population's childbearing age group, they contribute relatively few births.

Allen says migrants can also adopt the fertility patterns of their new country, which "in some cases, means even have lower fertility rates than the local population".

"Upon arrival in Australia, many migrants prioritise work and education, which delays family formation into their late 30s or beyond. This trend mirrors the broader patterns seen in the Australian population," she says.

Adelaide-based photographer Naina Redhu says the realities of parenthood are often underestimated. Credit: Supplied

For Adelaide-based freelance photographer Naina Redhu, moving to Australia meant meeting her partner, Jamie. While she says she is happy with her partner, neither of them wants to have children.

The 46-year-old says she has always been clear that she doesn't want children. Yet the decision has often prompted questions and unsolicited advice, including suggestions that she freeze her eggs as a precaution.

"My ex-husband and I were clear that we did not want children, but later, he did want to have kids some years down the line," she tells SBS Punjabi.

This is a fundamental choice; it narrates what kind of life you are choosing for yourself.

"I think it is selfish to have kids, and we ended up parting ways."

Redhu says not having a child doesn't mean she takes motherhood lightly.

"I believe parenting is a 24X7 commitment for the rest of your life. For someone like me, it would mean putting everything aside and being completely focused on raising the child, and I am not ready for that commitment yet," she says.

"There are so many things that I have to do and still want to do."

The barriers to having children

Allen says Australia should focus less on achieving an ideal number of children and more on removing hurdles that prevent people from having the families they want.

"We need to reach a point where having a much-wanted child, or a second child, is truly possible and not obstructed by barriers that feel insurmountable. Otherwise, the consequences ripple across society," she says.

She warns that smaller families may also have broader social consequences, including greater pressure on individuals to provide care for ageing relatives or fewer family connections to rely on.

Ultimately, having a child is not just a mother's responsibility; it is a societal concern.

"Until we address major challenges including housing affordability, economic security, climate change, and gender equality, Australians may lack the confidence and hope needed to plan for the future."

title: Caught out in a record-breaking storm: Why we didn't see it coming
text:
IN BRIEF: Rainfall and flash floods in south-east Queensland on Thursday far exceeded forecasts.

Experts say that while weather forecasting is always improving, climate change has complicated things.

A freak storm tore through south-east Queensland on Thursday, dumping more than 200mm of rain in three hours, leading to flash floods and hundreds of State Emergency Service calls.

Between Wednesday and Friday morning, at least eight weather stations just north of Brisbane in the catchments of the Pine and Caboolture rivers recorded huge 48-hour rainfall totals exceeding 300mm, according to weather tracking site Weatherzone.

While initial forecasts from the Bureau of Meteorology (BoM) predicted that Thursday would be the wettest day of the week in parts of Queensland, the severity of the downpour was unprecedented. Monthly rainfall records were broken in Nambour on the Sunshine Coast, where a running total of 401mm to Friday morning broke the old October record of 370.6mm, and in Beerburrum, in the same region, where the running monthly total rainfall of 354.2mm broke the old October record of 311.5mm.

Earlier this week, the BoM was questioned over false rainfall predictions later revealed to be caused by Bogong Moth migration. There were other times when its forecasts were off track, including in August, when Queensland rain outpaced forecasts, and after the 2023-2024 summer, when the El Niño weather event the bureau had predicted failed to materialise.

Senior lecturer in climate science at the University of Melbourne, Andrew King, said that while weather forecasts have improved immensely over time, "that doesn't mean they're always perfect", especially when it comes to forecasting thunderstorms and rainfall.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Small-scale storms, which can dump a lot of rainfall and have major impacts, are still hard to predict precisely, as it's difficult to forecast exactly where they'll occur, and that can mean forecast accuracy suffers, even over short timeframes."

READ MORE Wet weather expected to peak later in the week in soaked state

Smaller weather events like the thunderstorms in Queensland over the past few days are harder to represent in the models meteorologists use to simulate the atmosphere, he said.

Dr Michael Barnes from Monash University's School of Earth, Atmosphere and Environment told SBS News that while there had been vast improvements to the technology used to forecast weather, there were "limits to what is physically possible".

"Events such as thunderstorms that deliver 200 millimetres of rain within 24 hours are driven by highly localised atmospheric processes," he said.

"When weather is highly localised, even a small error can mean the storm's path or location isn't forecast particularly well.

"We often cannot know exactly where those storms will form or how intense they will become."

Weather forecasts are improving

"A seven-day forecast today is about as accurate as a two-day forecast was 40 years ago," Barnes said.

"There have been three major drivers of improved weather forecasting: better scientific understanding, greater computing power, and more observations.

"Twenty years ago, a forecast might have said that moderate rain was expected tomorrow afternoon. Today, people have weather apps that provide hourly rainfall forecasts and detailed estimates of expected precipitation."

READ MORE The El Niño backdrop that could spell trouble off Australia's coast

But he said that also meant expectations of weather forecasting have become much higher.

King agreed that there were higher expectations on the BoM, which he said had "certainly" come under scrutiny in recent years.

"Part of that is because Australians are relatively knowledgeable about climate drivers such as El Niño and La Niña. However, that understanding can sometimes become oversimplified."

But he warned that general understanding can sometimes "oversimplify" complex systems.

"People often hear 'El Niño' and assume conditions will be hot and dry. In reality, El Niño merely increases the likelihood of those outcomes; it doesn't guarantee them."

READ MORE El Niños could be more common in our future unless we change course, research suggests

Many factors influence Australia's weather, including the Indian Ocean, the Southern Ocean, Antarctica and tropical regions to the north.

"El Niño and La Niña are only part of the picture," he said.

"To be fair to the Bureau, it has tried to shift attention away from a narrow focus on those weather events and encourage people to pay more attention to seasonal outlooks, which incorporate all these influences."

SBS News has contacted the BoM for comment.

Climate change 'complicates' perceptions

When it comes to severe weather events, Barnes said, climate change "complicates things".

"Particularly in situations like the recent event in south-east Queensland, there is good evidence that daily and even sub-daily rainfall extremes are intensifying, primarily driven by thunderstorms," he said.

Produced by "the inherent chaos of the atmosphere", thunderstorms would continue to be challenging to predict.

While climate change doesn't necessarily reduce meteorologists' technical ability to forecast weather, it can affect how forecast accuracy is perceived.

Difficult-to-predict weather phenomena, such as localised severe thunderstorms, may be becoming "more consequential".

"As a result, it can appear that forecasts are becoming less reliable when, in reality, the impacts are increasing," Barnes said.

King from the University of Melbourne said climate scientists had discussed the tendency for "El Niño to become a scapegoat for everything that's happening in the climate system".

When people see severe weather during a strong El Niño, they naturally assume El Niño is the cause; however, climate change is operating in the background and is amplifying many extreme weather events.

"Climate change hasn't gone away. It's continuing to worsen as greenhouse gas emissions increase."

And climate change is "already" making extreme weather events worse, particularly heatwaves, which in Australia are more intense, more frequent and longer-lasting because of climate change.

But he said that as Australia's weather worsened, he understood the tendency to attribute severe weather to big events like El Niño and La Niña.

"There's a natural human desire to make sense of things that are difficult to understand," he said.

"Weather and climate are complicated, and reality is often more complex than it first appears."

title: Why millions of overseas basketball fans are following Sydney's newest star
text:
In Brief Chinese Olympian Yang Shuyu has brought millions of followers' attention to the WNBL.

Four Chinese national team players and a new broadcast deal are growing the league's reach in China.

A Chinese Olympian with more than five million online followers has made a winning start to life in Australia, helping the Sydney Flames to a dominant victory while drawing fresh attention to the Women's National Basketball League (WNBL) from fans across China.

Yang Shuyu scored 20 points in her first home game for the Flames on Saturday, helping guide the club to a 95-68 win over the Adelaide Lightning.

But the 24-year-old's arrival is about more than one player.

Yang — who has 5.3 million followers on Douyin, the Chinese equivalent of TikTok — is one of four Chinese national team stars in the league this season, as the WNBL looks to strengthen its presence in China and reach new audiences across Asia.

From China to Sydney

Yang joined the Flames earlier this year after building an impressive career in China.

The guard represented China at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, helping the country's 3x3 team win bronze. She was also part of the squad that won the 2023 Women's Asia Cup.

Fans cheer during the Sydney Flames' season opener, which drew a record opening-round crowd for the club. Source: Supplied

Speaking to SBS Mandarin, Yang said the move to Australia was driven by a desire to experience a different style of basketball.

"I've always wanted to play in different countries and experience different systems and styles of basketball," she said.

"I think that can help me improve."

Yang said she was already enjoying life in Sydney, both on and off the court.

"It feels great, and the weather is really nice. Everyone has been very kind to me, and I'm really looking forward to joining this big family."

'Already a star'

The excitement surrounding Yang's arrival was evident before she even stepped onto the court.

The Flames' season opener drew the largest opening-round crowd in club history, with many supporters telling SBS Mandarin they had come specifically to watch the Chinese star play.

"We're here to watch the Sydney Flames and support Yang Shuyu," one fan said.

"We hope she plays well and we hope she enjoys living in Sydney."

Yang Shuyu's growing fanbase was on display at the Flames' season opener. Source: Supplied

Another supporter said Yang had already become one of China's most recognisable basketballers.

"She's already a star in our national team," they said.

"We hope she can make her mark in an overseas league and show what she can do."

The attention Yang generated was matched by her performance.

She finished with 20 points, three rebounds and a steal, tying with teammate Jaz Shelley as the game's leading scorer in the Flames' 27-point win.

Flames coach Renae Garlepp said Yang had already made an impression despite only recently joining the squad.

"I think she played really well, and I'm happy for her," Garlepp said.

READ MORE How a South Sudanese Australian basketball star finally made it to the NBA

"What's great about her goes beyond the way she plays basketball. She's fitted into the team so easily.

"She's a lovely person and genuinely wants to be a good teammate. We're very lucky to have her."

Australian league sees rise in new Chinese fans

Yang's arrival also reflects a broader push by the WNBL to strengthen its connection with Chinese basketball fans.

She's one of four Chinese national team players competing in the league this season, alongside Southside Melbourne Flyers' Wang Siyu and Geelong Venom pair Zhang Wanglai and Han Xu.

WNBL chief operations officer Justin Nelson said the league had already seen growing interest from new audiences.

"Excitingly, we saw a huge rise in new fans, especially coming out to support the four Chinese national players and the high number of Opals playing this season," he said.

The Flames' season opener attracted a record opening-round crowd as the WNBL reported rising attendance and engagement. Source: Supplied

According to the league, opening-round attendance was up 40 per cent on last season, while social media engagement also reached record levels.

The growing interest comes as the WNBL expands its footprint in China. Last week, the league announced a broadcast partnership with Chinese media company YIDA that will make every game of the 2026-27 season available across Douyin, RedNote, Kuaishou and WeChat.

Nelson said the league hoped basketball could help build stronger connections between Australia and China.

"We hope basketball can serve as a bridge between the two countries, creating new opportunities for sporting exchange and new points of connection between Chinese and Australian cultures," he said.

Yang said she hopes to play a role in that exchange during her time in Australia.

"I'm really looking forward to meeting local fans and taking part in community events," she said.

"I also hope to bring some Chinese basketball culture here and build connections through sport."

More than 130,000 degree-qualified jobs could be wiped out by AI within a decade, a sobering government report by the agency tasked with assessing the nation’s future skills has warned. Jobs and Skills Australia has forecast “around 139,000” fewer jobs requiring a university degree in 10 years, with four of the top 10 occupations for graduates of commerce/management and society and culture at “medium risk” of automation. Trades jobs are expected to peak in the coming decade as degree-qualified roles decline. Matthew Absalom-Wong Futurist Michael McQueen said studying the humanities or forgoing university for a trade will give people entering the workforce an advantage over those in “highly cognitive but repetitive roles”. Essential to future-proofing is letting go of the idea of “university as the ultimate and the ideal” and giving vocational jobs equal consideration, McQueen said. “It’s no longer a sensible paradigm.”

Advertisement

Within universities, the critical thinking and creativity engendered by arts degrees make them a good option, he said. “It’s a way of thinking more than the actual skills that you’re learning,” he said, cautioning against going to university “because it’s the right thing to do”. The JSA analysis earlier this month shows jobs that are popular with university graduates are among those at risk. Accounting and financial services (management and commerce), admin and HR (management and commerce), admin and HR (society and culture) and legal and insurance (society and culture) are among the top five occupations for graduates of both disciplines. They have also been deemed at medium risk of “complete displacement” from AI automation.

Advertisement

Management and commerce graduates’ other top occupational choices – advertising/media, sales and executive roles – have been rated at a low risk of AI replacement. For society and culture graduates, top occupations with a low risk of AI replacement include health, education and advertising/media. But a number of those occupations are rated as high risk of AI taking over some elements of the industry. Jobs and Skills’ acting commissioner Trevor Gauld said: “The future is not fixed.” “It is true that entry-level roles may have some exposure challenges. But what we know is that human judgment, expertise and adaptability remains crucial. You gain many of those skills through those entry-level pathways. So this is about choice. If we don’t choose to ensure that we maintain those entry-level roles, how will the next generation of workers develop those judgment skills?”

Advertisement

Advertisement

“When you look at the priorities in this nation right now, we’re talking about housing, we’re talking about the care economy,” he said. “We’re talking about a future made in Australia. Huge numbers of these roles require an apprenticeship or traineeship pathway. There is huge opportunity for really meaningful, well-remunerated work in a whole range of occupations with quite low exposure. “But even those occupations with higher exposure, we still need that human judgment, we still need that critical thinking.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. title: ‘Final piece of the puzzle’: Western Sydney Airport opens for business
text:
Advertisement

BusinessCompaniesWestern Sydney International ‘Final piece of the puzzle’: Western Sydney Airport opens for business Chris Zappone Updated October 25, 2026 — 1:40pm ,first published October 25, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The first commercial flight from Sydney’s – and Australia’s – newest international airport took off this morning from Western Sydney International bound for the Gold Coast. Flight JQ362, with 188 passengers, aviation enthusiasts and journalists on board, departed at 11.22am. Thirty places were reserved for Jetstar officials and journalists and the rest for the paying public. As it taxied on the lone runway in the late morning light, crowds of plane spotters jammed nearby hillsides to get a glimpse of history. A helicopter hovered nearby. The flight was filled with passengers wearing Jetstar and WSI hats, aviation super-fans, proud western Sydneysiders and the generally curious. After a flight of one hour and nine minutes, JQ362 landed at its destination.

Advertisement

George Rasho was proud to be on the first flight from the new airport. The Age On the flight, western Sydney-based businessman George Rasho said he specifically booked to be on the inaugural journey. It was important to Rasho because WSI represented demographics of western Sydney. “It feels like the government has heard our voices, giving us the privilege of having a nearby airport,” said Rasho. “I’m proud to know that we are now put on the map for the world – and for the world to see one of the most multicultural places on Earth [in western Sydney].”

Advertisement

The federal government, which has backed the airport, and the City of Sydney hope WSI will give travellers a new option with round-the-clock, curfew-free flights domestically and internationally. Qantas-owned Jetstar is also vying to fly from WSI to Bali. The low-cost carrier is flying Airbus A320s, which seats up to 188 passengers, forming part of Jetstar’s newer, more-efficient and easier-to-operate fleet. Loading Before the first flight, passengers expressed excitement, relief and a little curiosity about being on the historic journey. Madi Merc, who lives near the airport, booked places for herself and her three children.

Advertisement

“Being on the flight is everything,” she said. “I was nine years old when I moved to Australia.” “I grew up on the farms around us,” said Merc, who said she’s trained for half Ironman contests and participated in the runway run before the airport was open. “To fly out of here now feels like the final piece of the puzzle,” she said. “It’s absolutely wild to say that where cows and sheep once grazed, there’s now people flying around. It’s really cool.” Moreover, Merc said she faced a 20-minute drive to the airport instead of an hour.

Advertisement

Jetstar expects to fly up to 24 return services a week from WSI. That means up to 14 a week to Melbourne, daily services to the Gold Coast and three weekly to Brisbane. Related Article Aviation Wheels up for Australia’s newest major airport as first flight takes off The addition of WSI as a new point of demand within Australia’s network of airports was overshadowed by a sense of relief by passengers who milled around the lobby before tagging luggage and going through security to the gate. The airport’s clean, well-lighted space played host to a low-key celebratory atmosphere with T-shirts, press conferences and mascot. The day began with a First Nation’s smoking ceremony, and the sense of place was evident in the design and layout of the facility. As passengers boarded, Australia’s political class – past and present – gathered and spoke in a nearby gate. Speakers including Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and NSW Premier Chris Minns, but the crowded was also filled with figures who’d help realise the project of the airport.

Advertisement

Aviation influencer Julian Tseng flew from Melbourne and was able to claim the first seat on the first domestic flight. The inaugural flight at the brand new Western Sydney International Airport takes off as dignitaries watch. Audrey Richardson Tseng, who describes himself as a “bit of a geek”, said: “It’s a historical occasion, not just for Sydney but for all of Australia. It’s not every day you get to witness the opening of a new airport.” Jetstar CEO Steph Tully championed the airline’s role in bringing “more choice and low fares to western Sydney”. “This is an historic day for aviation in Australia,” she said.

Advertisement

“We’ve got a strong track record of opening up new markets, and western Sydney, one of the fastest growing regions in the country, is going to be one of the great ones.” The initial route map is fairly modest to start, but it should expand over time as WSI settles in alongside Kingsford Smith. Related Article Airports ‘Slow burn’: Western Sydney Airport’s real challenge awaits after launch Eventually, WSI looks set to cater mostly to budget and leisure travel, while Kingsford Smith remains the main hub for premium and business trips. To mark the start of flights from WSI and induce passengers to try the airport, Jetstar announced fare sales featuring WSI-Gold Coast one-way fares starting from $54, WSI-Melbourne from $61 and WSI-Brisbane from $65.

Advertisement

But with a new airport come new baggage rules for passengers. The one-way fares will feature Jetstar’s new policy in which every passenger receives an under-seat personal item and access to overhead bins incurs an additional fee. Those who purchase bin access will board the plane first. The first international service takes place on Monday when Air New Zealand operates its inaugural flights connecting WSI and Auckland. In keeping with the leisure focus of WSI, Fiji Airways will fly three times a week starting in March. Additionally, passengers from WSI will be able to fly to Singapore with Singapore Airlines in November, and to Ho Chi Minh City with VietJet early next year.

Advertisement

At the end of next year, Virgin partner Qatar Airways will fly three return services a week to Doha. VietJet also plans to add direct Bangkok services by November next year, pending regulatory approval. Qantas will operate eight flights a week to Brisbane and Melbourne beginning next year. Key points DANCE: The Australian Ballet return to the State Theatre with The Nutcracker

MUSIC: Louis Tomlinson puts on a big show at John Cain Arena

DANCE

The Nutcracker ★★★★

The Australian Ballet, Ian Potter State Theatre, Arts Centre Melbourne, until October 31 The State Theatre has reopened after 2½ years of renovations, and Arts Centre Melbourne is keen to reassure audiences that its familiar character survives. The Australian Ballet has taken the hint, returning home with Peter Wright’s The Nutcracker, created for Birmingham Royal Ballet in 1990: an old favourite offering reassurance on a suitably extravagant scale. Yuumi Yamada as Clara in The Nutcracker. Kate Longley John F. Macfarlane’s gigantic, dreamy designs seem almost to have grown out of the theatre. The Stahlbaums’ drawing room, swathed in dark red curtains, extends the auditorium’s crimson plush into the family Christmas party. With festive decorations glistering like seams of emerald in the shadows, the whole experience feels deliciously subterranean: a theatre and a household tucked into the same deep burrow. We’re all here underground together. Yuumi Yamada supplies the youthful enthusiasm this cosy fantasy needs. Her Clara, a ballet student dreaming herself into a ballerina, is eager, unguarded and winsomely adolescent, and her delight in everything has an attractive freedom. Jarryd Madden’s fatherly Drosselmeyer offers a steadying presence.

Advertisement

The finest enchantment in this version remains Wright’s reimagined version of the Dance of the Snowflakes at the end of the first act, led here by Isobelle Dashwood’s graceful Snow Fairy. On Saturday night, the second act sometimes felt rushed. The national dances were briskly dispatched, and the Waltz of the Flowers grew a little unruly, the ensemble’s lines scattering beneath Macfarlane’s overhead tangle of streamers. Intentional or otherwise, the visual rhyme was actually quite enjoyable: the flowers and their consorts seemed to have caught the delirium of the decoration. But the entrance of Sharni Spencer’s queenly Sugar Plum Fairy soon restored order. The battle beneath the Christmas tree impresses. Kate Longley The theatre itself still smells new. The seats are a considerable improvement, although the space between rows feels even more miserly than before. The additional aisles do, however, offer more accessibility. The gridlock in the stalls after the curtain comes down is now, I hope, a thing of the past. The acoustics require a more cautious verdict after one visit, but, still, Orchestra Victoria – led by Jonathan Lo – sounded very good to me, with a notably crisp brass section. Familiarity has its attractions and there is still plenty in this production – such as the battle beneath the Christmas tree – that impresses. On the other hand, after nearly two decades and five seasons in The Australian Ballet’s repertoire, this Nutcracker is starting to feel a little old-fashioned. The building has had its renovation – now for the ballet?

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann

Advertisement

MUSIC

Louis Tomlinson ★★★★

John Cain Arena, October 20 The screams that greet Louis Tomlinson give me a contact high. Die-hard fans have legged it to the barrier and thrust stage. The word “Lemonade” flashes on-screen, towering over Tomlinson and his five-piece band. He cuts an amiable, Gallagher-type figure in a puffy red jacket and jeans. Until he’s briefly engulfed in a confetti explosion. Louis Tomlinson performing at John Cain Arena on October 20. Richard Clifford Music videos are composed live, faces projected dystopia-large with film effects, high-contrast overlays or psychedelic sunflowers, with colour-saturated stage lights and even a synth-laser show for Broken Bones. It’s a leap from the opening act, Rum Jungle, the kind of Aussie indie group you play driving to the beach on P-plates with your mates.

Advertisement

Tomlinson gets somewhat swallowed in the production. The mixing does no favours, his piping, Arctic Monkeys-style vocals no match for thundering drums in songs like The Spark. He’s often lost in backing harmonies and the word-faithful crowd, unless it’s the pared-back cover of the Foo Fighters’ My Hero. But Tomlinson’s impeccable band shines. Oozing rock, they unify eclectic leaps from funk pop and acoustic ballads to nostalgic indie/Britpop like the Oasis-esque Saturdays and Franz Ferdinand-style dance riffs in Out of my System. Keyboard skips between plinking piano and glimmering synth as the guitarists and bassist pace like tigers to tumbling, chest-shaking beats and rip blistering solos. The word “Lemonade” flashes on-screen over Tomlinson and his five-piece band. Richard Clifford Tomlinson performs a pop persona perfectly. Gracious and grateful. Hand on heart, pointing to swooning fans. His grinning, Yorkshire-accented commentary is lightly peppered with profanities: “Loud as you fooken’ can!” In return, the One Direction star is utterly adored. For One Direction’s Night Changes, a sea of phones rise, recording intently. Tomlinson’s grim-faced guards have to pull him back from the barrier when ladies get grabby in the encore. I only wonder if he regretted the jacket in the fervent, feminine body heat filling John Cain Arena.

title: Big W has spent more than a decade in Kmart’s shadow. Can it pull off a comeback?
text:

Mother-of-two Jun Bei Liu visited Kmart just last week. Her trip to Kmart Chatswood Chase yielded new lunch boxes for the kids, organisational baskets and decorative trays, to go with some recently purchased Anko vases. Her 13-year-old son and his friend also paid a visit to the Sydney store. “They bought a pair of slides,” she said. “It’s the first time they’ve ever been to the shops by themselves.” Liu is lead portfolio manager of Ten Cap, which handles funds exceeding $1.6 billion and is invested in Kmart’s parent company, Wesfarmers, but not Woolworths, Big W’s owner. By contrast, her last visit to Big W was about seven years ago. She remembers the department store in Macquarie Centre as having a messy apparel section, harsh lighting with a “warehouse feel”, a limited homewares section, and is not in a hurry to revisit. “If I have to travel far and wide to find this store when it’s not convenient, and it doesn’t provide all the categories I need, why should I go there?” Big W’s sticky narrative as Australia’s runner-up discount chain is unfortunately yet inevitably defined by how it is dwarfed by its more impressive, domineering rival Kmart, which for more than a decade has cemented its crown as the nation’s preferred discount department store. Today, Big W’s national footprint (178 stores) is about half the size of Kmart’s (more than 300), after 30 store closures were announced in 2019. While Kmart consistently produces more than $1 billion in profits, Big W’s have been in a downward slide for several years, and sank to minus $33 million in the 2025 financial year.

Advertisement

Some wonder what parent company Woolworths intends to do with it. In early 2025, the supermarket group’s chief executive, Amanda Bardwell, reignited speculation that a sale or exit of Big W might be on the cards after announcing a strategic review of the “shape of its business portfolio”. Management are eager to impart that a corner has been turned. Big W swung back into the black in the latest financial year, turning a $64 million profit thanks to less heavy discounting, stronger clothing sales and a thriving marketplace business. “We’re still early days in our transformation,” said Big W managing director Dan Hake. “We’ve had an important milestone this financial year, which was to prove out that we can step up our game in product. We can be absolutely competitive on price, and we can be lean and consistent enough in our operations that we can still make a profit at the end of the year. That’s just step one.” Big W managing director Dan Hake is overseeing the discount department store’s turnaround. Audrey Richardson The turnaround strategy is simple: keep shelf prices low, put better-quality products on the shelf, and get more efficient. Big W’s traditional areas of strength (“the purpose of Big W is to make a real difference for families,” said Hake) have been primarily in its kids’ offering, a books department so formidable that local book store operators complain it undercuts their market share, and toy aisles full of Barbies, Lego sets, Pokémon cards and Bluey merch.

Advertisement

Much investment has been poured into clothing, health and beauty, and homewares departments. Change rooms at newly renovated stores are painted in colourful pastels and large enough to fit prams. “We know that families spend on their kids first,” said Hake. “But we also want mum to have a great experience.” Store layouts are being reconfigured and trialled. Big W’s Plumpton store, 45 kilometres west of Sydney CBD, is among a handful of newly renovated stores with semi-enclosed sections for beauty and tech that are as much about driving people to explore what’s on the shelf as it is about stemming theft. In apparel, some price points are in the single digits (children’s tees for $3). A budget version of the popular barrel leg-style jeans sells for $30. About 80 per cent of the womenswear range is now under $20. “We’re not famous for it yet, but I think there’s great value,” said Hake. “We will get the growth, and we will become more front of mind for customers.” Big W Plumpton has been renovated to carve out distinct sections for health and beauty and tech products. Audrey Richardson Big W’s inescapable challenge is that it is stuck playing catch-up to Kmart, which has turned its in-house brand Anko into a standalone brand. But Big W cannot replicate Kmart’s strategy of turning private label products into 85 per cent of sales; it must juggle the dual task of growing exclusive-label lines without cannabilising its role as a “house of brands”. Kmart has organised its business around a tight supply chain that takes globally trending designs, bulk-ordering from Asian manufacturers in huge quantities, and selling them in Australia en masse. Its homewares and furniture department is so successful it has spawned an IKEA-like spin-off, K Home.

Advertisement

Shoppers on a budget, who have more price comparison tools today than ever, are choosing where to spend with ruthlessness. “If you’ve got a product and that product is even 10¢ cheaper at the competitor next door, that’s where they’re going to shop it. If quality is just a little bit off, and you’re trying to get away with saving costs in the wrong places, your customer is going to shop that product elsewhere,” said Hake. “These sound like little things, but to do it effectively at scale across the entire store, across all these different categories, it’s a big ask, right? You need to be absolutely on the ball.” It has demanded a broader cultural change across the organisation and a sharper focus on one united vision (“we are a price fighter on behalf of our customers”). More product designers and category managers have been brought in-house. “It’s a game of simplicity, stock flow, and just getting the basics right,” said Hake. Big W Plumpton is one of a handful of stores that have been renovated to entice shoppers. Audrey Richardson Where is Big W going? Big W’s position as runner-up goes deeper than mere numbers. Through Anko, Kmart’s offer to customers is unambiguous: designer-inspired products at budget prices. A loyal army of evangelists, in Facebook groups like Kmart Mums Australia or Kmart Home Decor & Hacks Australia, swap DIY hacks, styling tips and stock alerts with each other. “Kmart had a big hand in eliminating the bargain stigma, making it cool to shop there,” said RMIT University associate professor of marketing Dr Marian Makkar, pointing to “late night Kmart runs” becoming a social activity for teens and young adults.

Advertisement

Positioned as a “luxe-for-less” retailer, Kmart has gained cachet with Gen Z by delivering on style and aesthetic without the barrier of a high price tag, removing buyer’s remorse and increasing basket sizes, says Macquarie Business School marketing professor Jana Bowden. “That brand love for Kmart is the X factor,” said Bowden. “It’s what makes it different from its competitors. Kmart doesn’t just sell homewares and clothing. It sells a value consciousness, identity and a cultural moment.” It’s not clear how much time Hake has to execute Big W’s big turnaround. Rumours about the chain’s future have simmered for years. In August 2025, Bardwell announced Big W’s technology systems would be separated from Woolworths, a move often interpreted as preparing a business for potential demerging. Liu wonders if the market is big enough to accommodate many discount chains. Canadian giant Dollarama, which bought The Reject Shop early last year and is rebranding stores, runs a successful private label model that could threaten Kmart. “I really don’t know what that brand stands for, Big W,” Liu said. While a turnaround costs time and money, “how patient is Woolworths?” she asked. “You have to give it at least three years. I’m just not sure if Woolworths is that committed for [Big W] to turn around.” At Big W, Christmas began in September. Audrey Richardson

NationalNSWAviation Wheels up for Australia’s newest major airport as first flight takes off Matt O'Sullivan October 25, 2026 — 12:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
