At 11.22am, a Jetstar aircraft soared into blue skies from Western Sydney International Airport, marking the start of passenger flights and a new era for both Sydney and the country. Looking on from the departure gates at flight JQ362 bound for the Gold Coast were hundreds of guests, many of whom played a key role in the development of Australia’s first major new airport in half a century. Jetstar flight JQ362 on the tarmac moments before it is pushed back for the first flight. Audrey Richardson Moments earlier, from the departures area looking out to the Blue Mountains, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese officially marked the opening by unveiling a commemorative plaque and paying tribute to those who had played a part. “Everyone who has been part of this story along the way can feel proud today. It has been a long and remarkable journey for all of us,” he said.

Advertisement

Albanese said that the city had looked to the harbour and the CBD for too long, and the new $6 billion airport would turn that around to where people lived and worked in western Sydney. On Jetstar flight JQ362 was Gold Coast resident Mark Ignativ, 54, who was the first to check in physically in the terminal. “It’s rarer than a solar eclipse to be on the first flight from a new airport. It’s pretty unusual, especially in Australia,” he said. “I’ve been here when it’s only farms and houses. Now it’s finally open, it’s really a game changer. A city this size needs at least two airports.”

Advertisement

He admitted he was a “little bit” of an aviation enthusiast but “not the type that sit on ladders with telescopes”. He is heading back to western Sydney from the Gold Coast on the return Jetstar flight. Another on board was Hong Kong resident Jaing Liu, who flew to Sydney to join her daughter, TT Huang, to be part of history on the first flight. “This is a rare chance to be part of history. My mum is very excited,” said Huang, who lives in Sydney and describes herself as a plane enthusiast. TT Huang, left, and her mother, Jaing Liu, arrive at the airport to check in for the inaugural passenger flight. Audrey Richardson Flying the A320 out of the new airport were Jetstar captain Guy Proctor, 51, from the Gold Coast and first officer Aglaya Papadokokolakis, 25, from Blacktown.

Advertisement

“It’s definitely a privilege to have this opportunity. It’s a very special flight. To have the opportunity to fly out of an airport in my backyard is an amazing, amazing opportunity. It’s very special day,” Papadokokolakis said. The pilots are flying the return leg from the Gold Coast to the new airport. The inaugural passenger flight comes three months after cargo aircraft started flying to the curfew-free airport at Luddenham, on the city’s western fringe. Jetstar first officer Aglaya Papadokokolakis, 25, from Blacktown, and captain Guy Proctor, 51, from the Gold Coast outside the terminal. Audrey Richardson The airport is officially named after pioneering aviator Nancy-Bird Walton, known as the “Angel of the Outback”. It was fitting that among the guests was Walton’s daughter, Tweed, and the aviator’s granddaughters.

Western Sydney Airport chairman Paul O’Sullivan said the opening was the result of sustained conviction, adding that it had from benefited from bipartisan political support. “This is more than the opening of a building. It fulfils a nation-building promise to deliver a new 24-hour international gateway for Australia,” he said. “For decades, this airport existed only in the imagination of a small group of people with a bold vision. Today, that vision is a reality, and today is also evidence that Australia can deliver major infrastructure projects safely, on time and on budget.” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in the terminal on Sunday. Audrey Richardson Western Sydney Airport chief executive Simon Hickey said the airport was future-proofed and built to serve the city for the coming century. “When I think about that future, it’s genuinely difficult to fathom the impact Western Sydney International will have on greater Sydney,” he said.

Among guests were former prime ministers Tony Abbott and Scott Morrison, federal Labor ministers Chris Bowen, Don Farrell, Jason Clare and Michelle Rowland, as well as Premier Chris Minns and NSW governor-general Margaret Beazley. Abbott, who approved Badgerys Creek for the airport site in 2014, said it was his government that made the “final, irrevocable and definitive decision to make it happen”. A passenger in the check-in area before walking onto the first flight. Audrey Richardson Asked whether it would be a success, Abbott said it was likely to be a slow start before becoming the major airport for Sydney over the next 50 years due to its curfew-free status and growth in western parts. On Sunday, the airport also became a new tourist attraction as locals arrived to see the first flight, turning the terminal into a public space after years of largely being off limits during construction and fit-out.

City life Welcome to Western Sydney International Airport Jetstar chief executive Stephanie Tully said taxis or Uber rides for people travelling to Sydney’s Kingsford Smith Airport were often the most expensive part of the journey. “For the people that live in this area, it’s just a massive step change to access and frequency and departures. This airport provides a choice for people in NSW, which they’ve never had before,” she said. “Our Gold Coast service we increased frequency before we even took off. So that shows you there’s great demand for travel from people that live in this area.”

Air New Zealand will become the airport’s first international carrier on Monday when Flight NZ165 is due to arrive at 7.55am from Auckland, which will be followed over coming months by flights carried by Singapore Airlines, Vietnamese budget airline Vietjet and Fiji Airways. Last week, Qatar Airways became the fifth foreign airline to commit to serving the new airport, unveiling plans to operate three flights a week between Doha and western Sydney from late next year. Qantas will begin flying from the new airport on March 28 next year, operating four flights a week to both Melbourne and Brisbane using Embraer E190 aircraft. Cape Town: Matt Renshaw batted against the brand new ball in the Newlands nets as Cameron Green prepared to return to the Australian team for the pivotal third Test after the “really bizarre” abdominal injury that hijacked his tour. Green, who expressed a preference for batting Nos. 4 or 5 in the order but qualified this view by saying he was willing to bat anywhere for the team, also batted against a new ball in training on Saturday before continuing his return to the bowling crease with a centre-wicket spell. This week, however, he will play solely as a batsman. After two Tests batting at No.5, it looks like Matthew Renshaw will return to his customary position as opener in Cape Town. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe The injury in the ODI series had come at an unfortunate time for Green, immediately after he had asserted himself with runs and a clear batting method against Bangladesh in Darwin and Mackay. He strained a side muscle, more commonly associated with tennis, while trying to play a hook shot shortly after he was struck on the box in Potchefstroom. “It was really bizarre. I think there’s definitely a pretty clear link between getting hit and then doing the injury – I think it’s too much of a coincidence for them not to be related,” Green said. “I got hit where you don’t want to get hit, and then yeah, two balls later, I went to go just play a shot just behind the wicket.

“I had to lengthen my muscle, and I think my muscle was pretty keen to not move at that stage after I got hit. I think the stretching of the muscle … just had a tear through. “My immediate thoughts were talking to the medical staff and seeing what they thought, how long the timeline would be. And it’s quite a unique injury. There’s not many people that have done the injury but then tried to play a few weeks later, so they didn’t have much to go off. So I just stayed around the group until I’d heard further, depending on how I was tracking. Luckily enough, it’s all good to go for the last game.” Cameron Green copped a nasty blow in the third one day international match against South Africa in Potchefstroom last month and strained a side muscle shortly afterwards; an injury that kept him out of the first two Tests. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Green’s last collision with South Africa in a Test match was at the 2025 World Test Championship final in London last year, where he made a duck and four batting at No.3 – a bruising encounter with Kagiso Rabada. “It was a tough experience for sure,” Green said. “Pretty unique that you’re playing South Africa with the Dukes ball in England. I think there’s a lot of good learnings, a lot of tough learnings, but obviously they’re such a quality bowling line-up that you’ve got to be on your game at all times to succeed against them, regardless of where you bat.

“But certainly up the top of the order is incredibly difficult. I think because ... their opening bowlers … are so great with the new ball. So you’ve got to work really hard, especially at the start there.” Asked about where he preferred to bat, Green pointed strongly to the middle-order positions currently occupied by Steve Smith and Renshaw. title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
